365	points out that reported performance may not fully reflect
366	practical capability. This highlights the need for more robust
367	evaluation and training. IVDetect [41] performs vulnerability
368	detection with fine-grained interpretations. It improves feature
369	granularity. However, it does not directly target label-noise
370	correction. ReGVD [21] studies graph neural networks for
371	vulnerability detection and confirms the importance of graph-
372	based modeling. However, its learning process still assumes
373	conventional supervision. LineVul [42] uses a transformer-
374	based model for line-level vulnerability prediction. It improves
375	localization granularity. However, its effectiveness can still be
376	degraded by noisy annotations. Nie et al. [27] explicitly inves-
377	tigate label errors in deep-learning-based vulnerability detec-
378	tion and propose confidence learning and differential training
379	strategies. This work clearly shows that label noise is a non-
380	negligible issue in vulnerability datasets. SCL-CVD [43] im-
381	proves code vulnerability detection by supervised contrastive
382	learning with GraphCodeBERT. It strengthens discriminative
383	representations. However, it is designed for general software
384	rather than smart contracts. VulChecker [44] uses graph-based
385	vulnerability localization and data augmentation to improve
386	robustness. Its graph design is effective. However, it is still
387	not developed specifically for smart contracts. GCL4SVD
388	[45] estimates label-noise transitions through graph confident
389	learning and corrects mislabeled samples. It provides a useful
390	reference for noise-aware training. However, it is still targeted
391	at software vulnerability detection.
392	E. Comparison with Our Method
393	Table I gives a direct comparison between representa-
394	tive studies and our method. Existing program-analysis-based
395	methods have good interpretability, but they usually rely on
396	handcrafted rules or expensive path reasoning. Existing deep-
397	learning-based methods improve representation capability, but
398	most of them assume relatively reliable labels. Existing LLM-
399	based methods improve semantic analysis and explanation,
400	but their reliability is still limited in precise vulnerability
401	detection. Prior robust-learning studies also focus mainly on
402	general software rather than smart contracts. In contrast, our
403	method combines contrastive learning and granular-ball-based
404	robust training for smart contract vulnerability detection. The
405	contrastive part improves the discriminative quality of contract
406	representations, while the granular-ball mechanism improves
407	robustness under noisy supervision. Therefore, our method is
408	designed to achieve both robust representation learning and
409	vulnerability detection in smart contracts.
410	III. METHODOLOGY
411	This section illustrates our learning-based vulnerability de-
412	tection approach for smart contracts (i.e., CGBC), to fight
413	against label noise in training datasets, enhancing the robust-
414	ness of smart contract vulnerability detection. CGBC initial-
415	izes and optimizes the contract encoder based on large-scale
416	unlabeled pertaining, focusing on generating close vector rep-
417	resentations for similar smart contracts. Subsequently, CGBC
418	groups smart contracts to create coarse-grained labels and
419	representations during fine-tuning, to correct noisy labels. The
420	workflow of CGBC is illustrated in Figure 1, consisting of two
421	main procedures: (1) contrastive learning-based representa-
422	tion initialization, which introduces a semantic-preserving ap-
423	proach to augment smart contracts, and the extended datasets
424	will pretrain the model without labels based on contrastive
425	learning, to initialize smart contract representation through
426	considering label consistency. (2) Robust vulnerability detec-
427	tion by Granular-ball training, which instruments a Granular-
428	ball computing layer between the encoder layer and the clas-
429	sifier layer, to generate coarse-grained representations through
430	similarity distance-based clustering, further optimized through
431	a label-resilient symmetric cross-entropy loss function and a
432	two-dimensional clustering loss function. After training con-
433	vergence, CGBC derives a robust smart contract vulnerability
434	model despite noisy training datasets.
435	A. Contrastive Learning-based Representation Initialization
436	This module focuses on pretraining the model through un-
437	supervised contrastive learning, based on large-scale positive
438	sample pairs. By this procedure, on the one hand, the model
439	can generate more precise vector representations for smart
440	contracts; on the other hand, the representations of similar
441	smart contracts will be closer.

884	IV. EXPERIMENTAL EVALUATION
885	To comprehensively evaluate the effectiveness and robust-
886	ness of CGBC, we design a series of experiments aimed at
887	answering the following three research questions:
888	• RQ1: How effective is CGBC in detecting smart contract
889	vulnerabilities compared to state-of-the-art methods?
890	• RQ2: How do the core components of CGBC contribute to
891	its performance?
892	• RQ3: How robust is CGBC under different noise levels to
893	detect vulnerabilities in smart contracts?
894	• RQ4: How effective is Granular-ball computing for cluster-
895	ing in smart contracts?
896	A. Experimental Setup
897	Datasets. To comprehensively evaluate the effectiveness of
898	CGBC in detecting smart contract vulnerabilities, we cu-
899	rate training and evaluation datasets as follows: (1) Large-
900	scale and Representative Source: The dataset should originate
901	from publicly accessible, large-scale corpora that represent
902	diverse real-world smart contracts. (2) Verified Vulnerability
903	Labels: For fine-tuning and evaluation, contracts must be
904	annotated with confirmed vulnerability types (e.g., reentrancy,
905	integer overflow/underflow, timestamp dependency). (3) Tool-
906	Detectable Weaknesses: The labeled vulnerabilities should
907	be detectable by mainstream static analysis tools to ensure
908	compatibility and reproducibility. Our experiments leverage
909	three key datasets. For pretraining, we adopt Ethereum-SC
910	Large [9], a comprehensive corpus with over 113,000 raw
911	smart contracts. After preprocessing to remove invalid and
912	duplicate entries, 78,211 contracts remain for self-supervised
913	representation learning. During fine-tuning, we use a labeled
914	dataset from [10], which contains approximately 40,000 real-
915	world smart contracts annotated with major vulnerability types
916	such as reentrancy, integer overflow/underflow, and timestamp
917	dependency. For evaluation, we aggregate contracts from two
918	widely accepted benchmarks: ReentrancyBenchmark [9] and
919	SolidiFiBenchmark [9]. These datasets provide verified labels
920	derived from manual annotation and static analysis tools.
921	Each vulnerability type is represented by a binary label per
922	contract, where 0 indicates secure and 1 indicates vulnerable.
923	The vulnerability detection is conducted at the contract level.
924	To elude data leakage across the pretraining, fine-tuning and
925	testing sets, we identify and remove their overlapping samples.
926	Specifically, we normalize source codes and compute their
927	SHA-256 hashes to detect identical contracts. This check
928	proves the isolation of the testing set and identifies 4,781
929	groups of identical contracts between pre-training and fine-
930	tuning sets; these duplicates were removed from the fine-
931	tuning data to ensure strict separation. Intra-set duplication
932	was also detected, with 1,265 redundant groups in the pre-
933	training set and 204 in the fine-tuning set, all of which were
934	subsequently deleted.
935	Implementation Details. To ensure the effective extraction of
936	semantic and structural information from smart contracts, we
937	design a contract encoder based on a multi-layer Transformer
938	architecture. The encoder operates on tokenized contract se-
939	quences with a maximum length of 512 and is trained with a
940	masking strategy that encourages the model to infer contextual
941	relationships between tokens under partially observable input.
942	This setting strengthens the model’s ability to capture latent
943	code semantics and function-level dependencies, which are
944	essential for vulnerability detection. Following the encoder,
945	we stack several fully connected layers to refine the learned
946	representation and project it into a latent space suitable for
947	downstream classification. The model processes two views
948	of the same input contract in parallel, enforcing representa-
949	tion consistency across syntactically different but semantically

Robust Smart Contract Vulnerability Detection via Contrastive
Learning-Enhanced Granular-ball Training
Zeli Wang, Qingxuan Yang, Shuyin Xia, Yueming Wu, Bo Liu, Longlong Lin
Abstract—Blockchain has become the fundamental infrastruc-
ture for building a digital economy society. As the key technology
to implement Blockchain applications, smart contracts face
serious security vulnerabilities. Deep neural networks (DNNs)
have emerged as a prominent approach for detecting smart
contract vulnerabilities, driven by the growing contract datasets
and advanced deep learning techniques. However, DNNs typically
require large-scale labeled datasets to model the relationships
between contract features and vulnerability labels. In practice,
the labeling process often depends on existing open-sourced tools,
whose accuracy cannot be guaranteed. Consequently, label noise
poses a significant challenge for the accuracy and robustness
of the smart contract, which is rarely explored in the liter-
ature. To this end, we propose Contrastive learning-enhanced
Granular-Ball smart Contracts training, CGBC, to enhance
the robustness of contract vulnerability detection. Specifically,
CGBC first introduces a Granular-ball computing layer between
the encoder layer and the classifier layer, to group similar
contracts into Granular-Balls (GBs) and generate new coarse-
grained representations (i.e., the center and the label of GBs)
for them, which can correct noisy labels based on the most
correct samples. An inter-GB compactness loss and an intra-
GB looseness loss are combined to enhance the effectiveness of
clustering. Then, to improve the accuracy of GBs, we pretrain
the model through unsupervised contrastive learning supported
by our novel semantic-consistent smart contract augmentation
method. This procedure can discriminate contracts with different
labels by dragging the representation of similar contracts closer,
assisting CGBC in clustering. Subsequently, we leverage the sym-
metric cross-entropy loss function to measure the model quality,
which can combat the label noise in gradient computations.
Finally, extensive experiments show that the proposed CGBC can
significantly improve the robustness and effectiveness of the smart
contract vulnerability detection under various noisy settings when
contrasted with baselines.
Index Terms—Granular-ball, vulnerability detection, deep
learning, smart contract.
I. INTRODUCTION
B
LOCKCHAIN is a distributed and decentralized ledger
technology, which has been widely applied across var-
ious domains [1], [2]. Smart contracts, which serve as the

core mechanism for automating and enforcing business logic
on blockchain platforms, have become indispensable for en-
abling these applications. However, the prevalence of security
vulnerabilities in smart contracts remains a major obstacle,
significantly hindering the broader adoption and real-world
deployment of blockchain-based solutions [3]–[5]. Vulnerabil-
ity detection is a widely studied approach to enhancing smart
contract security. Traditional program analysis methods often
depend on manually defined vulnerability patterns, which are
constrained by expert knowledge and struggle to scale with
the intricate logic semantics of smart contracts [6]–[8]. Deep
learning offers a promising solution by automatically learning
vulnerability patterns through its powerful pattern recognition
capabilities [9]–[13].
MTVHunter leverages multiple teacher models to guide the
training process by aggregating their predictions into more
accurate soft labels, improving robustness and accuracy [13].
Clear achieves significant detection accuracy improvements
by generating labeled contract pairs through data sampling
and extracting semantic features using a Transformer module,
followed by model fine-tuning for vulnerability detection
[12]. Although these learning-based models have achieved
remarkable performance in detecting smart contract vulner-
abilities, their effectiveness relies on extensive high-quality
labeled datasets. In practice, existing smart contract datasets
are generally annotated by open-source tools [9], [10], [12]
However, the accuracy of current contract vulnerability detec-
tion tools is far from expectations: for example, the empirical
study on 47,587 contracts and nine tools demonstrate that
only 42% of contract vulnerabilities are detected [14]; the
research conducted on 18 contract detection tools proves that
they have poor performance. Consequently, the existing tool-
based label procedure will inevitably introduce much label
noise, which can significantly degrade model performance
[15]. Thus, mitigating the impact of label noise on learning-
based vulnerability detection is urgent.
Much research has been conducted to resolve the label noise
in computer vision [16], [17] and natural language processing
[18], [19], but only a few studies explore this problem in soft-
ware vulnerability detection. ACGVD [20] adopts a framework
that combines GNN and GAT, constructing a comprehensive
graph representation that integrates various types of informa-
tion from source code. This approach mitigates the noise in-
terference that may arise from relying on a single information
source, enhancing the model’s ability to adapt to complex
data. [21] designs adaptive graph convolution operations that
allow the model to adjust to noisy patterns automatically, and
employs a weighted loss function to mitigate the impact of
noisy labels. These tools demonstrate that deep learning-based

JOURNAL OF LATEX CLASS FILES, VOL. 18, NO. 9, SEPTEMBER 2020
2
vulnerability detection methods in traditional software systems
are susceptible to label noise and propose effective mitigation
strategies. However, these approaches cannot be directly gener-
alized to smart contracts due to their fundamental differences,
such as programming languages and logical architectures. To
the best of our knowledge, no countermeasures have been
proposed to address label noise in smart contract vulnerability
detection frameworks.
An intuitive way to address this problem is to identify and
correct noisy labels. However, it is nontrivial and computation-
ally exhaustive to spot all noisy labels precisely. To alleviate
this dilemma, bearing the core observation that most samples
are correctly annotated, we aim to cluster similar smart con-
tracts and remove noise through the centers of clusters, which
represent the common features and most labels. There are
two key challenges to achieve this goal: (1) generating close
embeddings for similar contracts. The embeddings of smart
contracts determine their similarity, namely, the correctness
of clustering. Since smart contracts have complicated code
structures and diverse user-defined variables, it is tricky to
embed contracts with the same labels closely. (2) Adaptively
clustering smart contracts. Smart contracts even belonging to
the same category may have distinct representative features.
This implies that smart contracts should be clustered according
to their data distribution features, rather than strictly clustering
the contracts with the same label into a set. Such requirements
ask for an adaptive multi-granularity clustering approach.
To overcome these challenges, we propose a novel robust
training approach for learning-based smart contract detection
models through contrastive learning-enhanced Granular-ball
computing (CGBC). Our CGBC achieves coarse-grained rep-
resentation learning through a Granular-ball (GB) clustering
layer. The label and vector representation of a GB center
are the new coarse-grained representation for all samples
in the current GB. This procedure can correct noisy labels
and diminish their influence. To address the first challenge
and bring similar contracts closer, we pretrain CGBC with
unsupervised contrastive learning to optimize the embeddings
of smart contracts. Additionally, we introduce the intra-GB
compactness loss and inter-GB looseness loss function to
the fine-tuning loss function to further pull the embeddings
of similar contracts closer. For the second challenge, we
adopt the Granular-ball computing method, an adaptively
multi-granularity clustering algorithm, to automatically group
smart contracts following data distribution features, without
predefined parameters such as the amount or size of sets.
By integrating these designs, CGBC realizes robust vulner-
ability detection for smart contracts. We conduct extensive
experiments on a large-scale dataset across three common
vulnerability types: Reentrancy (RE), Timestamp Dependency
(TD), and Integer Overflow (IO). The results demonstrate that
CGBC significantly improves the robustness of smart contract
vulnerability detection under label noise. Even with 40% noisy
labels, CGBC maintains high performance with an average F1-
score of 76.59%, outperforming all baseline methods. These
findings confirm the effectiveness and robustness of CGBC
in addressing label noise, enhancing the reliability of smart
contract analysis. To sum up, the contributions of this paper
are listed as follows:
• We
present
the
first
contrastive
learning-enhanced
Granular-ball training method for robust learning-based
smart contract vulnerability detection under noisy envi-
ronments, which leverages unsupervised pretraining to
initialize contract representations, and then uses coarse-
grained representation learning to mitigate label noise in
vulnerability detection.
• We propose a semantic-preserving smart contract aug-
mentation to conduct contrastive learning. Furthermore,
we introduce a Granular-ball-based coarse-fine robust
training method, assisted by intra-GB and extra-GB qual-
ity metrics for Granular-balls, to conduct robust learning
for smart contract vulnerability detection.
• Experimental results on abundant evaluations demonstrate
the effectiveness and robustness of our proposal. More-
over, our proposal always outperforms state-of-the-art
models.
II. RELATED WORK
This section reviews prior studies on smart contract vul-
nerability detection. Existing work can be classified into four
main categories, namely program analysis, deep learning, large
language models, and robust vulnerability detection. To make
the comparison clearer, Table I summarizes representative
studies and our method in terms of main work and remarks.
A. Program Analysis Method
Program analysis are classifical methods to detect smart
contract vulnerabilities. They are still widely used because
they provide clear semantic reasoning and good interpretabil-
ity. Oyente [22] explores execution paths by symbolic execu-
tion and uses SMT solving to detect vulnerabilities such as
reentrancy and arithmetic bugs. Its main strength is path-level
semantic analysis. However, it suffers from path explosion
and high analysis cost. SmartCheck [28] transforms Solidity
code into XML format and detects suspicious patterns through
XPath rules. This design is simple and efficient. However,
its detection ability depends on predefined rules. Slither [23]
performs static analysis by extracting structural information
such as abstract syntax and dependency relations. It is practical
and widely used. However, it still relies heavily on handcrafted
rules and may miss complex semantic vulnerabilities. Securify
[29] checks whether contract behaviors satisfy compliance
and violation patterns. It provides clear reasoning results.
However, its performance depends on the completeness of
manually designed security patterns. eThor [30] performs
sound static analysis for Ethereum smart contracts based on
Horn-clause reasoning. It provides stronger theoretical support.
However, this comes with higher analysis complexity. VerX
[24] verifies safety properties through symbolic execution
and delayed predicate abstraction. It is suitable for contracts
with high security requirements. However, it requires formal
property modeling and has high verification cost. EthPloit [25]
combines fuzzing with taint analysis and feedback guidance
to generate exploit-oriented test cases. It can better validate
triggerable vulnerabilities than pure static analysis. However,

B. Deep Learning Method
Deep learning has become an important direction for smart
contract vulnerability detection because it can learn vulner-
ability patterns from contract data automatically. Existing
studies mainly focus on graph modeling, transfer learning,
multimodal fusion, and contrastive representation learning.
The method in [31] models smart contracts as graphs and
performs vulnerability detection through structural representa-
tion learning. It shows the value of graph semantics. However,
early graph models are still limited in feature richness and
robustness design. AME [26] combines graph neural networks
with interpretable graph features and expert patterns. It bal-
ances representation learning and interpretability. However,
its reliance on expert-designed knowledge may reduce flex-
ibility. DLVA [9] extracts control-flow graphs and applies
graph convolutional networks for vulnerability analysis. It
improves structural modeling ability. However, it mainly fo-
cuses on graph topology and does not directly address noisy
supervision. ContractWard [5] develops automated vulnera-
bility detection models for Ethereum smart contracts in the
TNSE context. It shows the effectiveness of learning-based
detection. However, robustness to label noise is not its main
focus. ContractGNN [3] constructs vulnerability subgraphs
and uses graph neural networks for Ethereum smart contract
vulnerability detection. This design improves vulnerability-
oriented representation. However, it still assumes relatively
reliable labels during training. Cross-Modality [10] transfers
knowledge from source code to bytecode through a teacher–
student mutual learning framework. Its main strength is cross-
modal knowledge transfer. However, noisy annotations are
not explicitly modeled. ESCORT [32] improves vulnerability
detection through deep transfer learning and supports better
generalization to unseen vulnerabilities. This is useful in low-
resource settings. However, transfer learning alone cannot
solve noisy-label effects. EFEVD [33] enhances feature extrac-
tion by clustering contracts and learning graph embeddings for
contract communities. It strengthens contract representation
at the community level. However, it still relies on standard
supervision. CLEAR [12] introduces contrastive learning to
improve the discriminative quality of smart contract represen-
tations. It shows the value of contrastive objectives. However,
it does not explicitly address robust training under noisy
supervision. Vulnsense [34] integrates source code, opcodes,
graph structures, and language modeling for multimodal vul-
nerability detection. Its multimodal design enriches semantic
information. However, the framework is relatively complex
and still depends on label quality.
C. LLM-assisted Smart Contract Security Analysis
Large language models have recently been introduced into
smart contract security research. PSCVFinder [35] applies
prompt tuning to smart contract vulnerability detection. This
shows that prompt-based methods can support contract anal-
ysis. However, the method still depends on the stability of
prompt inference. SmartGuard [36] enhances vulnerability
detection with LLM-assisted analysis. Its main advantage
is stronger semantic understanding. However, reliability and
hallucination control remain major issues. SCALM [37] uses
large language models to identify bad practices in smart con-
tracts. This broadens the scope of contract analysis. However,
it is less specialized for precise vulnerability discrimination.
Smart-LLaMA-DPO [38] improves explainable smart contract
vulnerability detection with a reinforced large language model.
Its explainability is attractive. However, stable security judg-
ment still requires stronger task-specific robustness.

D. Robust Method
Label noise is a practical issue in vulnerability detection
because many datasets are automatically labeled by analyz-
ers, scanners, or heuristic rules. SySeVR [39] shows that
syntax-aware and semantic-aware representations can improve
vulnerability detection. Its representation design is effective.
However, noisy labels are not explicitly handled. Reveal
[40] revisits deep-learning-based vulnerability detection and
points out that reported performance may not fully reflect
practical capability. This highlights the need for more robust
evaluation and training. IVDetect [41] performs vulnerability
detection with fine-grained interpretations. It improves feature
granularity. However, it does not directly target label-noise
correction. ReGVD [21] studies graph neural networks for
vulnerability detection and confirms the importance of graph-
based modeling. However, its learning process still assumes
conventional supervision. LineVul [42] uses a transformer-
based model for line-level vulnerability prediction. It improves
localization granularity. However, its effectiveness can still be
degraded by noisy annotations. Nie et al. [27] explicitly inves-
tigate label errors in deep-learning-based vulnerability detec-
tion and propose confidence learning and differential training
strategies. This work clearly shows that label noise is a non-
negligible issue in vulnerability datasets. SCL-CVD [43] im-
proves code vulnerability detection by supervised contrastive
learning with GraphCodeBERT. It strengthens discriminative
representations. However, it is designed for general software
rather than smart contracts. VulChecker [44] uses graph-based
vulnerability localization and data augmentation to improve
robustness. Its graph design is effective. However, it is still
not developed specifically for smart contracts. GCL4SVD
[45] estimates label-noise transitions through graph confident
learning and corrects mislabeled samples. It provides a useful
reference for noise-aware training. However, it is still targeted
at software vulnerability detection.
E. Comparison with Our Method
Table I gives a direct comparison between representa-
tive studies and our method. Existing program-analysis-based
methods have good interpretability, but they usually rely on
handcrafted rules or expensive path reasoning. Existing deep-
learning-based methods improve representation capability, but
most of them assume relatively reliable labels. Existing LLM-
based methods improve semantic analysis and explanation,
but their reliability is still limited in precise vulnerability
detection. Prior robust-learning studies also focus mainly on
general software rather than smart contracts. In contrast, our
method combines contrastive learning and granular-ball-based
robust training for smart contract vulnerability detection. The
contrastive part improves the discriminative quality of contract
representations, while the granular-ball mechanism improves
robustness under noisy supervision. Therefore, our method is
designed to achieve both robust representation learning and
vulnerability detection in smart contracts.
III. METHODOLOGY
This section illustrates our learning-based vulnerability de-
tection approach for smart contracts (i.e., CGBC), to fight
against label noise in training datasets, enhancing the robust-
ness of smart contract vulnerability detection. CGBC initial-
izes and optimizes the contract encoder based on large-scale
unlabeled pertaining, focusing on generating close vector rep-
resentations for similar smart contracts. Subsequently, CGBC
groups smart contracts to create coarse-grained labels and
representations during fine-tuning, to correct noisy labels. The
workflow of CGBC is illustrated in Figure 1, consisting of two
main procedures: (1) contrastive learning-based representa-
tion initialization, which introduces a semantic-preserving ap-
proach to augment smart contracts, and the extended datasets
will pretrain the model without labels based on contrastive
learning, to initialize smart contract representation through
considering label consistency. (2) Robust vulnerability detec-
tion by Granular-ball training, which instruments a Granular-
ball computing layer between the encoder layer and the clas-
sifier layer, to generate coarse-grained representations through
similarity distance-based clustering, further optimized through
a label-resilient symmetric cross-entropy loss function and a
two-dimensional clustering loss function. After training con-
vergence, CGBC derives a robust smart contract vulnerability
model despite noisy training datasets.
A. Contrastive Learning-based Representation Initialization
This module focuses on pretraining the model through un-
supervised contrastive learning, based on large-scale positive
sample pairs. By this procedure, on the one hand, the model
can generate more precise vector representations for smart
contracts; on the other hand, the representations of similar
smart contracts will be closer.
1) Smart Contract Augmentation
The fundamental principle of contrastive learning is con-
structing positive sample pairs. Conducting data augmentation
on smart contracts is an intuitive way to achieve this. However,
it is nontrivial because of the complicated business logics and
syntax structures of smart contracts. Our core insight is to
insert a compilable contract-free code snippet s into a random
location Loc of the original contract C, which can maintain
the functionality of C in such a case. Specifically, according
to the syntax structure of smart contracts, the generation of
such a s must firstly declare new variables s1, then create
operation codes s2 on these variables to realize contract-free,
without interfering with the control and data dependencies
of the raw contract C. The operations are optional, which
will be created after being randomly chosen. We can obtain

and s2. Figure 2 presents the overall contract augmentation

indicating the access attributes such as ‘public’, ‘private’,
and ‘internal’, and a variable type TYPE. Subsequently, a
random variable name VAR and value VALUE are generated.
This process is formalized as MOD TYPE VAR = VALUE.
Until now, the generated statements s1 can act as a code
snippet s. To further diversify the augmentation samples,

semantic correctness but also introduces substantial structural
variation, providing a solid foundation for effective contrastive
representation learning.

B. Robust Vulnerability Detection by Granular-ball Training

notated smart contracts to endow the model with vulnerability
detection ability. To diminish the influence of label noise in

create coarse-grained representations and labels for training
samples, improving robustness. This procedure consists of two
main steps, namely contract Granular-ball construction and
loss-guided vulnerability detection optimization.

with the same label, the center of it represents the universal
and effective features of samples in the current GB. Bearing
the core insight that noisy labels are inevitable but are the
minority in the large-scale dataset, the embedding and label of
all samples in a GB are represented by the GB center and label,
respectively. This can improve robustness, but its performance
on smart contract vulnerability detection is limited to the
accuracy of new coarse-grained representations. To address

IV. EXPERIMENTAL EVALUATION
To comprehensively evaluate the effectiveness and robust-
ness of CGBC, we design a series of experiments aimed at
answering the following three research questions:
• RQ1: How effective is CGBC in detecting smart contract
vulnerabilities compared to state-of-the-art methods?
• RQ2: How do the core components of CGBC contribute to
its performance?
• RQ3: How robust is CGBC under different noise levels to
detect vulnerabilities in smart contracts?
• RQ4: How effective is Granular-ball computing for cluster-
ing in smart contracts?
A. Experimental Setup
Datasets. To comprehensively evaluate the effectiveness of
CGBC in detecting smart contract vulnerabilities, we cu-
rate training and evaluation datasets as follows: (1) Large-
scale and Representative Source: The dataset should originate
from publicly accessible, large-scale corpora that represent
diverse real-world smart contracts. (2) Verified Vulnerability
Labels: For fine-tuning and evaluation, contracts must be
annotated with confirmed vulnerability types (e.g., reentrancy,
integer overflow/underflow, timestamp dependency). (3) Tool-
Detectable Weaknesses: The labeled vulnerabilities should
be detectable by mainstream static analysis tools to ensure
compatibility and reproducibility. Our experiments leverage
three key datasets. For pretraining, we adopt Ethereum-SC
Large [9], a comprehensive corpus with over 113,000 raw
smart contracts. After preprocessing to remove invalid and
duplicate entries, 78,211 contracts remain for self-supervised
representation learning. During fine-tuning, we use a labeled
dataset from [10], which contains approximately 40,000 real-
world smart contracts annotated with major vulnerability types
such as reentrancy, integer overflow/underflow, and timestamp
dependency. For evaluation, we aggregate contracts from two
widely accepted benchmarks: ReentrancyBenchmark [9] and
SolidiFiBenchmark [9]. These datasets provide verified labels
derived from manual annotation and static analysis tools.
Each vulnerability type is represented by a binary label per
contract, where 0 indicates secure and 1 indicates vulnerable.
The vulnerability detection is conducted at the contract level.
To elude data leakage across the pretraining, fine-tuning and
testing sets, we identify and remove their overlapping samples.
Specifically, we normalize source codes and compute their
SHA-256 hashes to detect identical contracts. This check
proves the isolation of the testing set and identifies 4,781
groups of identical contracts between pre-training and fine-
tuning sets; these duplicates were removed from the fine-
tuning data to ensure strict separation. Intra-set duplication
was also detected, with 1,265 redundant groups in the pre-
training set and 204 in the fine-tuning set, all of which were
subsequently deleted.
Implementation Details. To ensure the effective extraction of
semantic and structural information from smart contracts, we
design a contract encoder based on a multi-layer Transformer
architecture. The encoder operates on tokenized contract se-
quences with a maximum length of 512 and is trained with a
masking strategy that encourages the model to infer contextual
relationships between tokens under partially observable input.
This setting strengthens the model’s ability to capture latent
code semantics and function-level dependencies, which are
essential for vulnerability detection. Following the encoder,
we stack several fully connected layers to refine the learned
representation and project it into a latent space suitable for
downstream classification. The model processes two views
of the same input contract in parallel, enforcing representa-
tion consistency across syntactically different but semantically

B. Overall Evaluations
Evaluations on RQ1: Effectiveness in detecting vulnera-
bility. Table III reports the results of 16 vulnerability detec-
tion methods on three common smart contract vulnerabilities:
Reentrancy (RE), Timestamp Dependency (TD), and Integer
Overflow (IO). We use recall (R), precision (P), and F1-
score (F) as evaluation metrics. All baseline results are taken
from [12], [51]. For fairness, CGBC is trained and tested on
the same datasets. Some tools, such as Osiris, Oyente, and
Securify, do not support all vulnerability types, so their results
are only reported on the tasks they cover.
We first compare CGBC with seven rule-based static anal-
ysis tools. These methods mainly rely on handcrafted rules,
so they often struggle with complex contract logic. CGBC
clearly outperforms them on all supported tasks. For RE,
CGBC reaches an F1-score of 94.74%, while Slither obtains
73.97%. For TD, CGBC achieves 97.14%, much higher than
SmartCheck’s 59.73%. For IO, CGBC reaches 98.36%, far
above Mythril’s 66.80%. These results show that CGBC can
capture vulnerability patterns more effectively than rule-based
tools.
Next, we compare CGBC with five advanced deep learning
methods. Although these methods learn better features than
static tools, they are still affected by label noise and lim-
ited contract semantics. Among them, DMT gives the best
average F1-score, which is 86.14%. CGBC achieves 96.75%,
improving the average F1-score by 10.61%. The gain on IO is
especially large, reaching 17.23%. This result suggests that the
coarse-grained Granular-ball representation helps the model
learn more robust features. We also compare CGBC with
LineVul, a general pretrained code model. Its average F1-score
is 76.57%, which shows that directly using a general code
model is not enough for smart contract vulnerability detection.

1	GBmooer: Granular-ball Text Label Smoothing with Hypersphere
2	Contrastive Learning
3	Jintao Zhaia, Zeli Wanga,∗, Shuyin Xiaa and Longlong Linb
4	aChongqing Key Laboratory of Computational Intelligence, Key Laboratory of Big Data Intelligent Computing, Key Laboratory of Cyberspace Big Data
5	Intelligent Security, Ministry of Education, College of Computer Science and Technology, Chongqing University of Posts and Telecommunications,
6	Chongqing, 400065, China
7	bCollege of Computer and Information Science, Southwest University, Chongqing, 400715, China
8	A R T I C L E I N F O
9	Keywords:
10	Granular-ball
11	Label Noise
12	Natural Language Processing
13	Text Classification
14	A B S T R A C T
15	Text label noise is pervasive and can significantly degrade the performance of natural language pro-
16	cessing (NLP) tasks. Traditional label smoothing is a commonly used mitigation technique, but most
17	existing methods rely solely on pre-trained models and perform a one-time global label smoothing
18	across the entire training dataset. This approach may introduce additional noise due to error accu-
19	mulation in the pre-trained models. To address this issue, we propose a novel data-adaptive multi-
20	granularity label smoothing framework, GBmooer. This method divides the latent space into locally
21	high-density regions represented by granular spheres, which are generated through a density-guided
22	iterative splitting process. Each granular sphere serves as a local normal prototype, where the sam-
23	ples within naturally maintain category consistency while also being tolerant to noisy samples. During
24	training, GBmooer first designs an unsupervised contrastive learning strategy based on hyperspheres,
25	which maps sample representations into hyperspherical space, resulting in a latent space that is con-
26	ducive to describing granular spheres. The optimized sample representations then guide the generation
27	of granular spheres with category consistency. Subsequently, GBmooer dynamically adopts a multi-
28	scale label smoothing strategy based on the label distribution within each granular sphere, helping
29	the model better combat label noise. Extensive experiments conducted under various noise condi-
30	tions demonstrate that GBmooer consistently outperforms current state-of-the-art baseline models.
31	Furthermore, when this framework is transferred to different backbone models, it still achieves sig-
32	nificant and stable performance improvements, fully demonstrating its excellent generalization ability
33	and transferability.
34	1. Introduction
35	The performance of deep neural networks (DNNs) heav-
36	ily relies on high-quality massive datasets. The performance
37	of deep neural networks (DNNs) heavily relies on high-
38	quality massive datasets, especially in complex learning sce-
39	narios such as graph representation learning and commu-
40	nity analysis Ye et al. (2026); He et al. (2024). However, in
41	practical applications, label noise is widely spread in train-
42	ing datasets, leading DNNs to overfit abnormal feature–label
43	mapping relationships and consequently compromising their
44	performance and generalizability Zhang et al. (2021); Arpit
45	et al. (2017).
46	As a result, countermeasures against label
47	noise have attracted widespread attention across a diverse
48	array of domains, including computer vision (CV) and natu-
49	ral language processing (NLP) (details in Section 2), as well
50	as other learning paradigms such as crowdsourcing and data
51	quality enhancement Hu et al. (2023). Notably, within the
52	realm of NLP, labels frequently exhibit a marked degree of
53	subjectivity and ambiguity, particularly in tasks such as sen-
54	timent analysis and text classification Liu et al. (2016); De-
55	vlin et al. (2019); Kim (2014). Besides, NLP demonstrates
56	a high level of sensitivity to label noise present in pretrained
57	models Zhang et al. (2022a); Zhu et al. (2022). As a conse-
58	quence, addressing label noise in NLP is crucial and urgent,
59	∗Corresponding author.
60	S240201075@stu.cqupt.edu.cn ( Jintao Zhai); zlwang@cqupt.edu.cn (
61	Zeli Wang); xiasy@cqupt.edu.cn ( Shuyin Xia); longlonglin@swu.edu.cn (
62	Longlong Lin)
63	especially under more realistic noise settings such as open-
64	set noisy labels Zhang et al. (2025).
65	Recently, several studies have been explored to relieve
66	the text label noise (Section 2), including approaches that
67	explicitly filter or correct noisy annotations based on noise
68	estimation or instance difficulty Li & Mao (2023); Hu et al.
69	(2023). One of the most popular methods is to leverage
70	label smoothing to fight against label noise Cheng et al.
71	(2023b); Qiao et al. (2022); Xu et al. (2024); Qi et al.;
72	Cheng et al. (2024). For example, Cheng et al. Cheng et al.
73	(2023b) pretrains the model and combines prediction proba-
74	bilities with original labels to adjust label confidence, form-
75	ing confidence-aware soft labels dynamically. Qiao et al.
76	Qiao et al. (2022) conducts multiple forward passes on each
77	sample during pretraining and mixes the prediction proba-
78	bilities to produce smoothed label distributions, reducing re-
79	liance on any single erroneous label. However, most exist-
80	ing related methods rely on pretraining the model over the
81	entire noisy dataset to generate initial pseudo-labels, caus-
82	ing the inherent learning bias from noisy labels to propagate
83	into and degrade the accuracy of label smoothing (Section
84	4).
85	To overcome this dilemma, we aim to combat label noise
86	by conducting localized label smoothing on groups of sim-
87	ilar samples. Compared to label smoothing based on super-
88	vised pretraining, such an approach can enhance the speci-
89	ficity and effectiveness of smoothing through data-driven lo-
90	cal adaptation, specifically on noisy datasets. However, to
91	J. Zhai et al.: Preprint submitted to Elsevier
92	Page 1 of 15
93	This preprint research paper has not been peer reviewed. Electronic copy available at: https://ssrn.com/abstract=6022343
94	Preprint not peer reviewed
95	
96	realize this goal, we face the following two key challenges.
97	(1) How to generate close embeddings for samples with
98	the same label? The fundamental goal of grouping sim-
99	ilar samples is to aggregate intra-class samples within the
100	same sets and separate inter-class samples across different
101	sets, by measuring the proximity between their embeddings.
102	However, the proximity between text representations does
103	not strictly correlate with their label consistency. For exam-
104	ple, in sentiment analysis, the embeddings of "I like eating
105	apple [Positive]" and "I don’t like eating apple [Negative]"
106	are proximate, but they have different labels; the embeddings
107	of "This movie is great [Positive]" and "The strawberries are
108	delicious [Positive]" are different sharply, but they have the
109	same label. Moreover, a significant disparity in any single
110	dimension between samples can be easily weakened in high-
111	dimensional vector spaces, due to “curse of dimensional-
112	ity". To realize effective clustering, optimizing sample rep-
113	resentations to enforce proximity among samples with iden-
114	tical labels is particularly essential in practical scenarios. (2)
115	How to implement localized label smoothing that simulta-
116	neously enhances model robustness and preserves accu-
117	racy? Existing approaches typically leverage a globally pre-
118	trained model on noise-corrupted datasets to guide smooth-
119	ing, which may introduce new noise due to learning biased
120	smoothed representations. Although improving robustness,
121	such global smoothing often compromises the accuracy of
122	the models Qi et al.; Qiao et al. (2022). Thus, constraining
123	smoothing to localized embedding subspaces could mitigate
124	this limitation.
125	To this end, in this paper, we propose GBmooer, a
126	novel multi-granularity label smoothing framework lever-
127	aging Granular-ball clustering and hypersphere contrastive
128	learning. GBmooer aims to introduce fewer perturbations by
129	narrowing the scope of label smoothing, thereby enhancing
130	model robustness while preserving correctness. Specifically,
131	for the first challenge, GBmooer introduces a hypersphere-
132	based contrastive learning to yield representations that re-
133	flect label distribution discrepancies, where intra-class sam-
134	ples exhibit geometric proximity while inter-class samples
135	maintain separation in the embedding space.
136	In particu-
137	lar, we first launch data augmentations on training sam-
138	ples to construct positive and negative samples. All sam-
139	ple embeddings are 𝓁2-normalized onto a unit hypersphere,
140	enabling similarity measurement by angular distance be-
141	tween feature vectors.
142	Compared to Euclidean or cosine
143	distance, the angle distance more stably characterizes the
144	high-dimensional semantic structure and facilitates the dis-
145	crimination of sample pairs in contrastive learning (details
146	in Section 3.1). For the second challenge, we adaptively
147	cluster training samples into multi-granularity sets based
148	on the optimized representations, and the label smooth-
149	ing is iteratively conducted on these Granular-balls respec-
150	tively. Namely, Granular-ball clustering can adaptively or-
151	ganize data at different granularities while preserving local
152	semantic consistency. Each Granular-ball contains semanti-
153	cally similar samples that theoretically share consistent la-
154	bels. Based on this, the label smoothing is performed in-
155	dependently for each Granular-ball, according to its inter-
156	nal label distribution. This loosely-coupled, multi-granular
157	label-smoothing approach effectively confines the risk im-
158	pact scope. In a nutshell, our main contributions are high-
159	lighted as follows:
160	Novel Label Smoothing Framework. We propose a novel
161	multi-granularity label smoothing model, GBmooer, to re-
162	lieve text label noise, based on Granular-ball clustering en-
163	hanced by the hypersphere-based contrastive learning.
164	Effective Algorithms. The hypersphere-based contrastive
165	learning proposed can effectively optimize representation
166	to distinguish the decision boundaries between different
167	classes. Meanwhile, our proposed Granular-ball-based lo-
168	calized label smoothing algorithm can effectively combat la-
169	bel noise by narrowing down the influence space of noise.
170	Extensive Experiments.
171	We conduct extensive exper-
172	iments on multiple text classification datasets, covering
173	various noise types, including class-conditional noise and
174	instance-dependent noise. In particular, these empirical re-
175	sults show that our method significantly outperforms exist-
176	ing general noise-handling approaches. Besides, we transfer
177	our method to foundational models (e.g., LSTM and GRU),
178	achieving superior results compared to corresponding noise-
179	robust methods, thereby demonstrating strong model trans-
180	ferability.
181	2. Related Work
182	Label Noise in CV. Numerous strategies have been pro-
183	posed in the literature to mitigate the impact of label noise
184	in CV. For example, Huang et al. improve noise detection
185	precision by enhancing the semantic separability of features
186	Huang et al. (2023). Northcutt et al. leverage estimated label
187	transition matrices and confidence scores to identify poten-
188	tial noisy samples Northcutt et al. (2021). Patrini et al. in-
189	corporate a regularization term into the loss function based
190	on noise distributions Patrini et al. (2017). Ma et al. propose
191	normalized loss functions to mitigate overfitting to noisy la-
192	bels Ma et al. (2020). More recently, contrastive learning
193	has emerged as an effective paradigm to alleviate the adverse
194	effects of label noise. For instance, Li et al. propose a self-
195	supervised contrastive learning framework that significantly
196	reduces the negative impact of noisy labels during training
197	Li et al. (2022). Chuang et al. introduce a robust train-
198	ing scheme employing a weighted InfoNCE loss, effectively
199	suppressing the interference from noisy views in representa-
200	tion learning Chuang et al. (2022). Although these proposals
201	have achieved great success in combating label noise in CV,
202	they cannot be directly applied to NLP because of the dis-
203	crete features of texts.
204	Label Noise in NLP. Compared to CV, research on label
205	noise in NLP has begun relatively recently. The work Jin-
206	dal et al. (2019) incorporates an additional noise-adaptive
207	layer to estimate label corruption probabilities and generate
208	soft pseudo-labels, which are then combined with clean su-
209	pervision to enable robust training. Song et al. Song et al.
210	J. Zhai et al.: Preprint submitted to Elsevier
211	Page 2 of 15
212	This preprint research paper has not been peer reviewed. Electronic copy available at: https://ssrn.com/abstract=6022343
213	Preprint not peer reviewed

266	ample, Cheng et al. Cheng et al. (2023a) propose the GB-
267	DP clustering algorithm. Xie et al. Xie et al. (2023) ap-
268	ply GBs to spectral clustering, effectively reducing the com-
269	putational cost and resource consumption when processing
270	high-dimensional data. GBC has been widely applied across
271	various domains, such as machine learning Xia et al. (2022,
272	2021); Yang et al. (2025b), graph neural networks Xia et al.
273	(2025c), computer vision Xia et al. (2025a), support vector
274	machine Quadir et al. (2025); Xia et al. (2025b), natural lan-

494	3.2. Granular-ball Label Smoothing
495	The goal of this module is to enhance the model’s ro-
496	bustness under textual label noise learning.
497	We propose
498	a multi-granularity label smoothing based on Granular-ball
499	computing. This approach can cluster similar samples into
500	a Granular-ball (GB), and all samples within a GB share the
501	common universal features. When applying label smooth-
502	ing on GBs, within a Granular-ball, the majority of correct
503	samples can weaken the influence of minority noisy samples.
504	The following will detail the procedure of the Granular-ball
505	clustering and the label smoothing.
506	3.2.1. Granular-ball Clustering
507	Granular-ball clustering (GBC) adaptively groups sam-
508	ples based on the similarity of sample representations. With-
509	out the constraints of cluster size or number, GBC yields
510	multi-granularity clustering results (i.e., GBs described in
511	Definition 3.1) that better reflect the underlying data distri-
512	bution. Here, ‘multi-granularity’ indicates that samples with
513	identical labels may be grouped into different GBs with un-
514	fixed sizes. Furthermore, to overcome the influence of label
515	noise and the complexity of high-dimensional computation
516	during clustering, we enhance the original GBC by an angle-
517	based unsupervised GBC. The details of the clustering pro-
518	cess are shown in Algorithm 1.

701	3.2.2. Label Smoothing
702	After Granular-ball clustering, the training dataset is
703	divided into multi-granularity Granular-balls 𝐺𝐵𝑠, which
704	form high-quality sets that follow the data distribution fea-
705	tures. According to the quality constraints of GBs, the em-
706	beddings of samples within the same GB exhibit high prox-
707	imity and label consistency. It implies that although each
708	Granular-ball may have several samples with label noise, this
709	only accounts for a small proportion. Therefore, an intuitive
710	countermeasure against label noise is to substitute the sam-
711	ple label with the majority label within the current GB, due
712	to the similarity of samples in a GB. However, this method
713	is too strict to be accurate, overlooking the influence of label
714	noise. Instead, we iteratively perform local label smooth-
715	ing in the granularity of Granular-balls. The label smooth-
716	ing on different Granular-balls is mutually independent and
717	does not interfere with each other. Specifically, the hard la-
718	bels of the samples in a GB are converted into soft labels,
719	based on the label distribution of the GB as shown in Defini-
720	tion 3.3. This approach prevents the model from overfitting
721	noisy samples, while preserving partial true-label informa-
722	tion for potential misclustered samples within a GB, thereby
723	enhancing the model’s learning accuracy. Furthermore, the
724	label smoothing within local GBs achieves a loose coupling
725	of the complete dataset, thereby reducing the influence of
726	noise.

GBmooer: Granular-ball Text Label Smoothing with Hypersphere
Contrastive Learning
Jintao Zhaia, Zeli Wanga,∗, Shuyin Xiaa and Longlong Linb
aChongqing Key Laboratory of Computational Intelligence, Key Laboratory of Big Data Intelligent Computing, Key Laboratory of Cyberspace Big Data
Intelligent Security, Ministry of Education, College of Computer Science and Technology, Chongqing University of Posts and Telecommunications,
Chongqing, 400065, China
bCollege of Computer and Information Science, Southwest University, Chongqing, 400715, China
A R T I C L E I N F O
Keywords:
Granular-ball
Label Noise
Natural Language Processing
Text Classification
A B S T R A C T
Text label noise is pervasive and can significantly degrade the performance of natural language pro-
cessing (NLP) tasks. Traditional label smoothing is a commonly used mitigation technique, but most
existing methods rely solely on pre-trained models and perform a one-time global label smoothing
across the entire training dataset. This approach may introduce additional noise due to error accu-
mulation in the pre-trained models. To address this issue, we propose a novel data-adaptive multi-
granularity label smoothing framework, GBmooer. This method divides the latent space into locally
high-density regions represented by granular spheres, which are generated through a density-guided
iterative splitting process. Each granular sphere serves as a local normal prototype, where the sam-
ples within naturally maintain category consistency while also being tolerant to noisy samples. During
training, GBmooer first designs an unsupervised contrastive learning strategy based on hyperspheres,
which maps sample representations into hyperspherical space, resulting in a latent space that is con-
ducive to describing granular spheres. The optimized sample representations then guide the generation
of granular spheres with category consistency. Subsequently, GBmooer dynamically adopts a multi-
scale label smoothing strategy based on the label distribution within each granular sphere, helping
the model better combat label noise. Extensive experiments conducted under various noise condi-
tions demonstrate that GBmooer consistently outperforms current state-of-the-art baseline models.
Furthermore, when this framework is transferred to different backbone models, it still achieves sig-
nificant and stable performance improvements, fully demonstrating its excellent generalization ability
and transferability.
1. Introduction
The performance of deep neural networks (DNNs) heav-
ily relies on high-quality massive datasets. The performance
of deep neural networks (DNNs) heavily relies on high-
quality massive datasets, especially in complex learning sce-
narios such as graph representation learning and commu-
nity analysis Ye et al. (2026); He et al. (2024). However, in
practical applications, label noise is widely spread in train-
ing datasets, leading DNNs to overfit abnormal feature–label
mapping relationships and consequently compromising their
performance and generalizability Zhang et al. (2021); Arpit
et al. (2017).
As a result, countermeasures against label
noise have attracted widespread attention across a diverse
array of domains, including computer vision (CV) and natu-
ral language processing (NLP) (details in Section 2), as well
as other learning paradigms such as crowdsourcing and data
quality enhancement Hu et al. (2023). Notably, within the
realm of NLP, labels frequently exhibit a marked degree of
subjectivity and ambiguity, particularly in tasks such as sen-
timent analysis and text classification Liu et al. (2016); De-
vlin et al. (2019); Kim (2014). Besides, NLP demonstrates
a high level of sensitivity to label noise present in pretrained
models Zhang et al. (2022a); Zhu et al. (2022). As a conse-
quence, addressing label noise in NLP is crucial and urgent,
∗Corresponding author.
S240201075@stu.cqupt.edu.cn ( Jintao Zhai); zlwang@cqupt.edu.cn (
Zeli Wang); xiasy@cqupt.edu.cn ( Shuyin Xia); longlonglin@swu.edu.cn (
Longlong Lin)
especially under more realistic noise settings such as open-
set noisy labels Zhang et al. (2025).
Recently, several studies have been explored to relieve
the text label noise (Section 2), including approaches that
explicitly filter or correct noisy annotations based on noise
estimation or instance difficulty Li & Mao (2023); Hu et al.
(2023). One of the most popular methods is to leverage
label smoothing to fight against label noise Cheng et al.
(2023b); Qiao et al. (2022); Xu et al. (2024); Qi et al.;
Cheng et al. (2024). For example, Cheng et al. Cheng et al.
(2023b) pretrains the model and combines prediction proba-
bilities with original labels to adjust label confidence, form-
ing confidence-aware soft labels dynamically. Qiao et al.
Qiao et al. (2022) conducts multiple forward passes on each
sample during pretraining and mixes the prediction proba-
bilities to produce smoothed label distributions, reducing re-
liance on any single erroneous label. However, most exist-
ing related methods rely on pretraining the model over the
entire noisy dataset to generate initial pseudo-labels, caus-
ing the inherent learning bias from noisy labels to propagate
into and degrade the accuracy of label smoothing (Section
4).
To overcome this dilemma, we aim to combat label noise
by conducting localized label smoothing on groups of sim-
ilar samples. Compared to label smoothing based on super-
vised pretraining, such an approach can enhance the speci-
ficity and effectiveness of smoothing through data-driven lo-
cal adaptation, specifically on noisy datasets. However, to
J. Zhai et al.: Preprint submitted to Elsevier
Page 1 of 15
This preprint research paper has not been peer reviewed. Electronic copy available at: https://ssrn.com/abstract=6022343
Preprint not peer reviewed

realize this goal, we face the following two key challenges.
(1) How to generate close embeddings for samples with
the same label? The fundamental goal of grouping sim-
ilar samples is to aggregate intra-class samples within the
same sets and separate inter-class samples across different
sets, by measuring the proximity between their embeddings.
However, the proximity between text representations does
not strictly correlate with their label consistency. For exam-
ple, in sentiment analysis, the embeddings of "I like eating
apple [Positive]" and "I don’t like eating apple [Negative]"
are proximate, but they have different labels; the embeddings
of "This movie is great [Positive]" and "The strawberries are
delicious [Positive]" are different sharply, but they have the
same label. Moreover, a significant disparity in any single
dimension between samples can be easily weakened in high-
dimensional vector spaces, due to “curse of dimensional-
ity". To realize effective clustering, optimizing sample rep-
resentations to enforce proximity among samples with iden-
tical labels is particularly essential in practical scenarios. (2)
How to implement localized label smoothing that simulta-
neously enhances model robustness and preserves accu-
racy? Existing approaches typically leverage a globally pre-
trained model on noise-corrupted datasets to guide smooth-
ing, which may introduce new noise due to learning biased
smoothed representations. Although improving robustness,
such global smoothing often compromises the accuracy of
the models Qi et al.; Qiao et al. (2022). Thus, constraining
smoothing to localized embedding subspaces could mitigate
this limitation.
To this end, in this paper, we propose GBmooer, a
novel multi-granularity label smoothing framework lever-
aging Granular-ball clustering and hypersphere contrastive
learning. GBmooer aims to introduce fewer perturbations by
narrowing the scope of label smoothing, thereby enhancing
model robustness while preserving correctness. Specifically,
for the first challenge, GBmooer introduces a hypersphere-
based contrastive learning to yield representations that re-
flect label distribution discrepancies, where intra-class sam-
ples exhibit geometric proximity while inter-class samples
maintain separation in the embedding space.
In particu-
lar, we first launch data augmentations on training sam-
ples to construct positive and negative samples. All sam-
ple embeddings are 𝓁2-normalized onto a unit hypersphere,
enabling similarity measurement by angular distance be-
tween feature vectors.
Compared to Euclidean or cosine
distance, the angle distance more stably characterizes the
high-dimensional semantic structure and facilitates the dis-
crimination of sample pairs in contrastive learning (details
in Section 3.1). For the second challenge, we adaptively
cluster training samples into multi-granularity sets based
on the optimized representations, and the label smooth-
ing is iteratively conducted on these Granular-balls respec-
tively. Namely, Granular-ball clustering can adaptively or-
ganize data at different granularities while preserving local
semantic consistency. Each Granular-ball contains semanti-
cally similar samples that theoretically share consistent la-
bels. Based on this, the label smoothing is performed in-
dependently for each Granular-ball, according to its inter-
nal label distribution. This loosely-coupled, multi-granular
label-smoothing approach effectively confines the risk im-
pact scope. In a nutshell, our main contributions are high-
lighted as follows:
Novel Label Smoothing Framework. We propose a novel
multi-granularity label smoothing model, GBmooer, to re-
lieve text label noise, based on Granular-ball clustering en-
hanced by the hypersphere-based contrastive learning.
Effective Algorithms. The hypersphere-based contrastive
learning proposed can effectively optimize representation
to distinguish the decision boundaries between different
classes. Meanwhile, our proposed Granular-ball-based lo-
calized label smoothing algorithm can effectively combat la-
bel noise by narrowing down the influence space of noise.
Extensive Experiments.
We conduct extensive exper-
iments on multiple text classification datasets, covering
various noise types, including class-conditional noise and
instance-dependent noise. In particular, these empirical re-
sults show that our method significantly outperforms exist-
ing general noise-handling approaches. Besides, we transfer
our method to foundational models (e.g., LSTM and GRU),
achieving superior results compared to corresponding noise-
robust methods, thereby demonstrating strong model trans-
ferability.
2. Related Work
Label Noise in CV. Numerous strategies have been pro-
posed in the literature to mitigate the impact of label noise
in CV. For example, Huang et al. improve noise detection
precision by enhancing the semantic separability of features
Huang et al. (2023). Northcutt et al. leverage estimated label
transition matrices and confidence scores to identify poten-
tial noisy samples Northcutt et al. (2021). Patrini et al. in-
corporate a regularization term into the loss function based
on noise distributions Patrini et al. (2017). Ma et al. propose
normalized loss functions to mitigate overfitting to noisy la-
bels Ma et al. (2020). More recently, contrastive learning
has emerged as an effective paradigm to alleviate the adverse
effects of label noise. For instance, Li et al. propose a self-
supervised contrastive learning framework that significantly
reduces the negative impact of noisy labels during training
Li et al. (2022). Chuang et al. introduce a robust train-
ing scheme employing a weighted InfoNCE loss, effectively
suppressing the interference from noisy views in representa-
tion learning Chuang et al. (2022). Although these proposals
have achieved great success in combating label noise in CV,
they cannot be directly applied to NLP because of the dis-
crete features of texts.
Label Noise in NLP. Compared to CV, research on label
noise in NLP has begun relatively recently. The work Jin-
dal et al. (2019) incorporates an additional noise-adaptive
layer to estimate label corruption probabilities and generate
soft pseudo-labels, which are then combined with clean su-
pervision to enable robust training. Song et al. Song et al.
J. Zhai et al.: Preprint submitted to Elsevier
Page 2 of 15
This preprint research paper has not been peer reviewed. Electronic copy available at: https://ssrn.com/abstract=6022343
Preprint not peer reviewed

Figure 1: Overview of 𝐺𝐵𝑚𝑜𝑜𝑒𝑟. It consists of two main stages: (1) in the contrastive
learning stage, the model is first pretrained based on positive and negative sample pairs
in the hypersphere, to learning high-quality textual feature representations; (2) in the
label smoothing stage, Granular-ball clustering groups these similar representations into
the same fine-grained clusters (i.e., Granular-balls). Based on the label distribution within
each Granular-ball, we perform label smoothing to mitigate the impact of noisy labels.
Finally, the refined feature representations along with the smoothed labels are fed into the
model to conduct training, based on KL divergence loss functions.
(2023) track the prediction behavior of samples across multi-
ple training stages to identify and retain reliable samples for
model updates. Han et al. (2018) train two networks simulta-
neously to select small-loss samples for the other, avoiding
overfitting noisy labels. Liu et al. (2020) introduces early-
learning regularization by constraining the prediction distri-
bution to remain close to its historical average, mitigating
the memorization of corrupted labels. On the other hand,
label smoothing is also effective in mitigating noise. For
example, Cheng et al. Cheng et al. (2023b) design label-
specific confidence estimation and pseudo-labeling mech-
anisms to dynamically adjust the training signal in multi-
label tasks, while Xu et al. Xu et al. (2024) propose label-
dependent selective denoising to smooth noisy labels, signif-
icantly improving performance under heterogeneous noise
distributions. Besides, Qiao et al. Qiao et al. (2022) fit
Gaussian mixture models to sample losses to estimate la-
bel noise transition matrices, enabling adaptive separation of
noisy samples and label smoothing. Qi et al. Qi et al. iden-
tify unreliable samples through prediction consistency de-
tection in training iterations, and apply confidence-weighted
softening or directly replace their labels with prediction dis-
tributions to achieve label smoothing correction. Although
these methods have made progress in mitigating label noise,
they face the challenges of distinguishing between clean and
noisy samples, as well as the risk of cumulative errors in
label smoothing. To address these issues, we introduce con-
trastive learning to enhance the discriminability of textual
representations and integrate granular-ball clustering to per-
form localized label smoothing based on sample distribu-
tion, effectively mitigating label noise.
Granular-ball Computing. Granular computing has shown
promising potential in handling uncertainty and complex
data. Building upon the theoretical foundation of granular
computing Chen (1982), Wang et al. propose the concept of
Granular Cognitive Computing Wang (2017). Based on this,
Xia et al. Xia et al. (2019) introduce Granular-ball Comput-
ing (GBC), which covers datasets using multiple Granular-
balls (GBs) defined by centers and radius. These GBs are
then used in place of the original samples for downstream
tasks, improving robustness. Much work has been proposed
to improve the efficiency and stability of GBC Cheng et al.
(2025); Xie et al. (2024, 2023); Xia et al. (2025d). For ex-
ample, Cheng et al. Cheng et al. (2023a) propose the GB-
DP clustering algorithm. Xie et al. Xie et al. (2023) ap-
ply GBs to spectral clustering, effectively reducing the com-
putational cost and resource consumption when processing
high-dimensional data. GBC has been widely applied across
various domains, such as machine learning Xia et al. (2022,
2021); Yang et al. (2025b), graph neural networks Xia et al.
(2025c), computer vision Xia et al. (2025a), support vector
machine Quadir et al. (2025); Xia et al. (2025b), natural lan-
J. Zhai et al.: Preprint submitted to Elsevier
Page 3 of 15
This preprint research paper has not been peer reviewed. Electronic copy available at: https://ssrn.com/abstract=6022343
Preprint not peer reviewed

guage processing Hu et al. (2025); Wang et al. (2024b); Su
et al. (2025), rough sets Xia et al. (2023); Chen et al. (2025);
Yang et al. (2025a). For instance, the work in Liu et al.
(2024) improves the robustness of machine learning mod-
els by enhancing their generalization from limited data. Xia
et al. Xia et al. (2020) propose the Granular-ball neighbor-
hood rough set method, which adapts Granular-ball neigh-
borhoods to improve model adaptability and robustness on
uneven data distributions.
In the context of natural lan-
guage processing, recent studies have explored leveraging
Granular-ball structures to enhance robustness against data
uncertainty. For example, Wang et al. Wang et al. (2024a)
employ Granular-ball based sample enhancement to defend
against adversarial textual perturbations, while Wang et al.
Wang et al. (2024b) further extend this idea to combat tex-
tual label noise through Granular-ball based robust training.
However, existing Granular-ball based methods mainly fo-
cus on robustness enhancement or noise suppression from a
training perspective, and how to explicitly exploit GBC for
label noise smoothing has not been explored, which consti-
tutes our first breakthrough on this matter.
3. Methodologies
In this paper, we take text classification as a represen-
tative task to illustrate our proposal. Given a noisy dataset

3.1. Hypersphere-based Contrastive Learning
Traditional granular sphere clustering methods typically
focus on forming local normal spheres through data den-
sity. However, when faced with the high-dimensional na-
ture and complex structure of text data, samples in the orig-
inal high-density regions often lack class consistency. As a
result, traditional granular sphere methods are difficult to di-
rectly apply to such data. The high dimensionality of text
data makes clustering methods in the original space less ef-
fective in capturing the inherent relationships between data
points. Therefore, to address this challenge, we first map the
text data into a latent space. This latent space better accom-
modates the complex structure of high-dimensional data and
provides representations that are more suited to the charac-
teristics of text data during the clustering process. Through
this encoding approach, we can effectively construct a suit-
able clustering latent space for high-dimensional, complex
text data.
Therefrom we propose a hypersphere-based contrastive
learning encoding method. By projecting the samples onto
the unit hypersphere, we obtain more uniform and discrim-
inative text representations in the high-dimensional space.
This encoding process effectively alleviates the problem of
class inconsistency within the same high-density region,
providing higher-quality text feature representations for the
subsequent clustering process, thereby laying a solid founda-
tion for label noise handling. Given a dataset 𝐷= {(𝑠𝑖

3.2. Granular-ball Label Smoothing
The goal of this module is to enhance the model’s ro-
bustness under textual label noise learning.
We propose
a multi-granularity label smoothing based on Granular-ball
computing. This approach can cluster similar samples into
a Granular-ball (GB), and all samples within a GB share the
common universal features. When applying label smooth-
ing on GBs, within a Granular-ball, the majority of correct
samples can weaken the influence of minority noisy samples.
The following will detail the procedure of the Granular-ball
clustering and the label smoothing.
3.2.1. Granular-ball Clustering
Granular-ball clustering (GBC) adaptively groups sam-
ples based on the similarity of sample representations. With-
out the constraints of cluster size or number, GBC yields
multi-granularity clustering results (i.e., GBs described in
Definition 3.1) that better reflect the underlying data distri-
bution. Here, ‘multi-granularity’ indicates that samples with
identical labels may be grouped into different GBs with un-
fixed sizes. Furthermore, to overcome the influence of label
noise and the complexity of high-dimensional computation
during clustering, we enhance the original GBC by an angle-
based unsupervised GBC. The details of the clustering pro-
cess are shown in Algorithm 1.

3.2.2. Label Smoothing
After Granular-ball clustering, the training dataset is
divided into multi-granularity Granular-balls 𝐺𝐵𝑠, which
form high-quality sets that follow the data distribution fea-
tures. According to the quality constraints of GBs, the em-
beddings of samples within the same GB exhibit high prox-
imity and label consistency. It implies that although each
Granular-ball may have several samples with label noise, this
only accounts for a small proportion. Therefore, an intuitive
countermeasure against label noise is to substitute the sam-
ple label with the majority label within the current GB, due
to the similarity of samples in a GB. However, this method
is too strict to be accurate, overlooking the influence of label
noise. Instead, we iteratively perform local label smooth-
ing in the granularity of Granular-balls. The label smooth-
ing on different Granular-balls is mutually independent and
does not interfere with each other. Specifically, the hard la-
bels of the samples in a GB are converted into soft labels,
based on the label distribution of the GB as shown in Defini-
tion 3.3. This approach prevents the model from overfitting
noisy samples, while preserving partial true-label informa-
tion for potential misclustered samples within a GB, thereby
enhancing the model’s learning accuracy. Furthermore, the
label smoothing within local GBs achieves a loose coupling
of the complete dataset, thereby reducing the influence of
noise.

The GB clus-

𝑂(𝑏𝑑log (𝑏∕3)) = 𝑂(𝑏𝑑log 𝑏). Therefore, the time com-
plexity of the whole GB clustering is 𝑂(𝑁𝑑log 𝑁). The
cost of label smoothing within a GB is 𝑂(|𝐺𝐵|𝐶), where

steps, i.e., angular pretraining, granular-ball generation, la-

4. Experiments
To comprehensively evaluate the effectiveness of our
proposed method, we first conduct comparative experiments
with current state-of-the-art baselines on multiple datasets.
Building on this, we further design a series of in-depth exper-
iments to analyze the key mechanisms of our method, aiming
to answer the following six core research questions (RQs):
∙RQ1: How effective is GBmooer in combating label
noise, compared with state-of-the-art baselines?
∙RQ2: How do key components contribute to the per-
formance of GBmooer?
∙RQ3:
How effective is Granular-ball clustering,
specifically under the assistance of angular contrastive
learning?
∙RQ4: Is GBmooer sensitive to different hyperparam-

∙RQ5: Is GBmooer stable during training?
∙RQ6: How is the transferability of GBmooer across
different network architectures?
4.1. Experimental Setup
Datasets.
Experiments are conducted on four popu-
lar datasets:
TREC, AGNEWS, IMDB, and Chnsenti-
corp Voorhees & Tice (1999); Zhang et al. (2015); Maas
et al. (2011); Tan & Zhang (2008), where Chnsenticorp
is a Chinese-language dataset and the others are English-
language datasets. Table 1 shows more information about
the dataset.
These datasets will be further introduced to
two popular kinds of label noise (i.e., class-conditional noise
(CCN) and instance-dependent noise (IDN)) to evaluate the
robustness of our proposal. CCN contains symmetric (Sym)
and asymmetric (Asym) noise, where the former randomly
flips labels to any other class with equal probability, and the
latter flips labels only to classes that are semantically sim-
ilar to the original label. Since the IMDB and Chnsenti-
corp datasets are binary classification tasks, symmetric and
asymmetric noise are effectively equivalent. IDN depends
on individual sample features. Specifically, we first train an
LSTM-based classifier, then flip the labels to other labels
with the highest prediction probability. Due to the imbal-
anced and multi-class nature of the TREC dataset, IDN is
not applied to it. The noise ratios of CCN and IDN are both
set to 20 and 40 to evaluate all models’ performance.

We compare our proposal with the following

trains them differently; (5) Adaptive Cheng et al. (2023b),
which performs a pretraining to divide the dataset into sub-

Implementation Details. To avoid biases, all methods use
the same pretrained language model, namely BERT-Base-
