1640	5.3.2.  Assessment of key components
1641	Our proposed method introduces two core innovations: (1) a multi-
1642	level noise identiﬁcation strategy based on the G-ODT and S-ICD in-
1643	dicators, and (2) a beneﬁcial noise learning strategy with tailored loss 
1644	functions. To evaluate the individual contributions of these components, 
1645	we implement and test the following variants of our model. BNO-GB: 
1646	The full model with multi-level noise identiﬁcation (G-ODT and S-ICD) 
1647	and beneﬁcial noise learning using all three loss functions. w/o G-ODT 
1648	& S-ICD: a variant with noise identiﬁcation is removed. Training is per-
1649	formed on the full noisy dataset using standard softmax loss, and in-
1650	ference still adopts granular-ball-based decision boundaries. w/o 𝑑𝑖𝑠𝑝: 
1651	a variant with OOD Dispersion Loss is removed. w/o 𝑝𝑟𝑜𝑡𝑜: a variant 
1652	with Prototype Softmax Loss is removed. w/o 𝑚𝑎𝑟𝑔𝑖𝑛: a variant with 
1653	Prototype Margin Loss is removed.
1654	Table 6 presents the performance of all ablation variants on Stack-
1655	Overﬂow and SNIPS under the 25% known class ratio and 20% noise 
1656	setting. Experiments on the same dataset are conducted using the same 
1657	hyperparameter conﬁguration, and results are averaged over four dif-
1658	ferent random seeds for robustness. As shown in the Table 6, removing 
1659	any single component results in a performance drop, demonstrating that 
1660	each module makes a meaningful contribution to the overall eﬀective-
1661	ness of BNO-GB.
1662	5.4.  Analysis of G-ODT and S-ICD
1663	In Section 4.2, we proposed two indicators, G-ODT and S-ICD, and 
1664	used their values along with label information to make noise recogni-
1665	tion. To assess the discriminative capability of the proposed indicators, 
1666	we plot the probability density distributions of G-ODT and S-ICD values 
1667	for clean samples, IND noise, and OOD noise, categorized according to 
1668	ground-truth labels on the StackOverﬂow and SNIPS datasets, as shown 
1669	in Fig. 3 (a)-(d).
1670	Fig. 3(a) and (c) present the distribution of G-ODT values. It can 
1671	be observed that the G-ODT values of clean and IND noise samples 
1672	are primarily concentrated near zero, indicating that their correspond-
1673	ing granular-balls maintain label consistency with neighboring balls 
1674	and are positioned near the same-label balls in the feature space. In 
1675	contrast, the G-ODT values of OOD noise samples tend to be higher, 
1676	suggesting that their granular-balls deviate signiﬁcantly from known 
1677	classes. These results conﬁrm the eﬀectiveness of the G-ODT indica-
1678	tor in capturing out-of-distribution tendencies. Fig. 3(b) and (d) show 
1679	the S-ICD value distributions. Across both datasets, clean and IND noise 
1680	samples share similar distributions, with relatively high S-ICD values 
1681	concentrated on the right-hand side, whereas OOD noise samples ex-
1682	hibit signiﬁcantly lower S-ICD values concentrated in the left-hand re-
1683	gion. This indicates that the S-ICD indicator eﬀectively captures the 
1684	in-distribution consistency of samples, allowing for reliable noise-type
1685	diﬀerentiation.
1686	In summary, G-ODT and S-ICD provide complementary perspectives 
1687	at the granular-ball level and the sample level, respectively, for mod-
1688	eling outlier and inlier tendencies. Their distribution patterns not only 
1689	validate the discriminative ability of each individual indicator but also 
1690	demonstrate their synergistic potential in jointly enabling robust noise 
1691	identiﬁcation under open-world conditions.

1702	we conduct experiments on the StackOverﬂow dataset under a known 
1703	class ratio of 25% and a total noise ratio of 40%. Fig. 4(a)–(d) illus-
1704	trate how the model performance varies as 𝑝𝑡 increases from 0.5 to 0.9 
1705	in increments of 0.1, under diﬀerent ﬁxed values of 𝑛𝑡 set to 8, 10, 12, 
1706	and 14, respectively. The plots show the eﬀects of 𝑝𝑡 on four evaluation 
1707	metrics: Known, Open, F1-All, and Acc.
1708	The results reveal a consistent pattern, as the purity threshold in-
1709	creases, all performance metrics initially improve, indicating that ex-
1710	cluding low-purity granular-balls enhances the reliability and discrim-
1711	inative ability of the decision boundary. However, when 𝑝𝑡 becomes 
1712	too large (e.g., 𝑝𝑡= 0.9), a noticeable performance drop occurs in cer-
1713	tain settings, particularly in subﬁgure (d), with the Known and F1-score 
1714	metrics exhibiting sharp declines. This suggests that overly strict pu-
1715	rity constraints may result in insuﬃcient sample coverage, leading to 
1716	the exclusion of informative data during training. Moreover, as the size 
1717	threshold 𝑛𝑡 increases, the peak performance tends to shift toward lower 
1718	purity values, indicating that when the granular-ball size requirement

1720	tive generalization. It is also worth noting that across all subﬁgures, the 
1721	performance on unknowns (Open) is mostly the highest. This highlights 
1722	the eﬀectiveness of our Beneﬁcial Noise-guided Representation Learn-
1723	ing module in promoting open space representation, thereby enhancing 
1724	the model’s ability to recognize open intents.

1825	6.  Conclusions
1826	In this paper, we present a novel framework, BNO-GB, to tackle 
1827	open intent classiﬁcation in the presence of both IND and OOD noisy 
1828	labels. Speciﬁcally, we perform granular-ball clustering to obtain noise-
1829	robust granular-ball representations. In addition, we design a multi-
1830	level noise sample selection strategy by combining granular-ball-level 
1831	and sample-level indicators to accurately identify clean, IND noise, and 
1832	OOD noise samples. Furthermore, we develop a beneﬁcial noise-guided 
1833	learning strategy that leverages OOD noise to expand the open space, 
1834	while jointly enhancing class representation and inter-class separabil-
1835	ity through three tailored loss functions. Extensive experiments demon-
1836	strate the eﬀectiveness of our method across various noise scenarios. Al-
1837	though BNO-GB exhibits strong robustness under complex noise, several 
1838	parameters, including the granular-ball thresholds used in splitting and 
1839	inference, remain sensitive to the scale of the dataset. This introduces 
1840	limited manual conﬁguration when adapting to datasets of diﬀerent den-
1841	sities. In future work, we plan to develop adaptive or parameter-free 
1842	granular-ball mechanisms to automatically determine these thresholds. 
1843	We also aim to further improve computational eﬃciency and extend the 
1844	framework to broader open intent understanding scenarios.

Beneﬁcial noise learning for open intent classiﬁcation via granular-ball 
representation
Yanhua Li
, Xiaocao Ouyang
, Jie Zhang
, Chaofan Pan
, Lingfei Ren
, Xin Yang
∗
School of Computing and Artiﬁcial Intelligence, Southwestern University of Finance and Economics, 611130, Chengdu, China
a r t i c l e  i n f o
Keywords:
Beneﬁcial noise learning
Granular-ball computing
Open intent classiﬁcation
 
a b s t r a c t
Open intent classiﬁcation aims to correctly classify the known intents into their corresponding classes while iden-
tifying unknown intents. However, most existing methods assume clean training data, overlooking the prevalent 
label noise in real-world scenarios, including both in-distribution (IND) and out-of-distribution (OOD) noise. 
Moreover, existing noise-handling approaches typically rely on a single-criterion rule for identifying noisy sam-
ples, with limited consideration of neighborhood information, and they rarely explore the potential beneﬁts that 
noise may oﬀer for representation learning. To address these issues, we propose a Beneﬁcial Noise-guided Open 
Intent Classiﬁcation method via Granular-Ball Representation (BNO-GB). Speciﬁcally, we perform unsupervised 
granular-ball clustering to obtain noise-resistant granular-ball representations. Based on these representations, 
we design two complementary indicators, the Granular-ball-level Outlier Distribution Tendency (G-ODT) and 
the Sample-level Inlier Consistency Degree (S-ICD), to build a multi-level noise recognition scheme that sepa-
rates clean samples, IND noise, OOD noise, and uncertain cases. Using the identiﬁed noise types, we introduce 
a beneﬁcial noise-guided representation learning strategy. Extensive experiments across multiple datasets and 
noise conditions demonstrate the eﬀectiveness and robustness of our approach. The source code of BNO-GB is 
available at: https://github.com/Liyanhuaa/BNO_GB.
1.  Introduction
Open intent classiﬁcation [1] aims to enable a model not only to 
recognize known intents seen during training but also to detect novel, 
unseen intents at inference time, a capability that is essential for practi-
cal dialogue systems. However, training data collected from real-world 
applications often contains various forms of label noise, making this 
task substantially more challenging. The noise typically includes in-
distribution (IND) noise, where samples originating from known classes 
are mislabeled as other known classes, and out-of-distribution (OOD) 
noise, where samples from external distributions are incorrectly anno-
tated as known classes [2]. Both noise types disrupt the learning of stable 
representations for known intents and hinder the formation of a reliable 
boundary for unknown intents. A common line of work in noisy-label 
learning adopts a “sample selection followed by representation learn-
ing” paradigm [3,4], in which samples are ﬁrst distinguished accord-
ing to their noise type and then optimized with diﬀerentiated learning 
strategies.
Sample selection aims to partition training data into clean samples, 
IND noise, and OOD noise by assessing the reliability of each instance

renlf@swufe.edu.cn (L. Ren), yangxin@swufe.edu.cn (X. Yang).
through speciﬁc criteria. Representative methods typically rely on a sin-
gle criterion, such as small-loss selection [3], prediction consistency [5], 
or distance to prototypes [6]. While such criteria can work reasonably 
well in controlled settings, depending on a single type of evidence makes 
the decision process vulnerable to noisy or ambiguous samples. More-
over, most existing approaches overlook the use of neighborhood infor-
mation for noise identiﬁcation, ignoring the valuable cues embedded in 
local agreement and distribution deviation.
In the area of noisy-label representation learning, numerous strate-
gies have been proposed to improve robustness, including reweighted 
objectives [7], contrastive regularization [8], and noise-aware feature 
correction [9]. Beyond these techniques, an emerging line of research 
has highlighted the constructive role of noise. For instance, positive-
incentive noise reduces task complexity and facilitates more eﬀective 
optimization [10,11]; noise-driven augmentation is now viewed as an 
estimator of beneﬁcial noise that strengthens contrastive learning [12]; 
and structured beneﬁcial noise embedded into pretrained models sup-
ports incremental learning while preserving old-class discrimination 
[13]. These ﬁndings collectively reveal that noise can provide meaning-
ful learning signals. However, the beneﬁcial nature of noise has not yet

been explored in open intent classiﬁcation. Developing eﬀective ways 
to transform noisy samples into useful signals for open-world represen-
tation learning remains an important but unresolved challenge.
For sample selection, we draw inspiration from granular-ball com-
puting [14]. Granular-ball clustering [15] adaptively groups nearby 
samples into local units and represents the data distribution with a set of 
balls, each characterized by attributes such as centroid, radius, purity, 
and label. The label of a granular-ball is determined by the majority la-
bel of its contained samples, which naturally suppresses the inﬂuence of 
noisy labels and thus provides stronger robustness in high-noise scenar-
ios. More importantly, the attributes of a granular-ball, together with 
its relationships to neighboring balls, reveal many aspects of both the 
ball itself and the samples it contains. As illustrated in Fig. 1, which pro-
vides an example of the granular-balls derived from clustering, granular-
ball A is assigned the label “blue”, but its neighboring balls exhibit in-
consistent labels, and it also lies far from other balls sharing the label 
“blue”. This large deviation, together with its low purity, suggests that 
granular-ball A likely corresponds to a region dominated by OOD noise, 
and therefore samples 1-4 inside it have a high probability of being OOD 
noise. In contrast, granular-ball B shows high label agreement with its 
surrounding balls and exhibits high purity, indicating that it represents 
in-distribution samples. Based on the consistency between sample labels 
and the label of granular-ball B, sample 5 can be identiﬁed as IND noise, 
whereas samples 6–9 can be regarded as clean samples. Thus, granular-
ball representation enables the design of multi-perspective indicators for 
identifying noise types, which in turn supports more eﬀective represen-
tation learning.
Building on these observations, we introduce a Beneﬁcial Noise-
guided Open Intent Classiﬁcation method via Granular-Ball Represen-
tation (BNO-GB). Speciﬁcally, we perform granular-ball clustering in a 
label-agnostic and unsupervised manner to obtain granular-ball repre-
sentation of the training features, which alleviates the adverse impact 
of mislabeled samples. In addition, the granular-ball representation en-
ables us to design two complementary indicators from distinct view-
points, which collectively constitute a multi-level noise sample selection 
strategy. At the granular-ball level, we propose the Granular-ball-level 
Outlier Distribution Tendency (G-ODT) to estimate the likelihood that 
a granular-ball primarily consists of OOD noise. At the sample level, we 
design the Sample-level Inlier Consistency Degree (S-ICD) to measure 
how well a sample ﬁts the distribution of its assigned granular-ball. 
Combining these two indicators enables us to partition the data into 
clean samples, IND noise, OOD noise, and uncertain cases. Based on the 
identiﬁed noise types, we further develop a beneﬁcial noise-guided op-
timization scheme. The OOD Dispersion Loss allows OOD noise to act as 
a constructive signal for shaping the open region by encouraging sep-
aration between known intents and the potential unknown space. The 
Prototype Softmax Loss and the Prototype Margin Loss encourage clean 
and corrected IND samples to acquire more discriminative, class-speciﬁc 
representations. These objectives are jointly optimized to promote ro-
bust representation learning. Overall, the contributions of this work are 
as follows:
(1) We propose BNO-GB, a new framework for open intent classiﬁ-
cation under noisy conditions, which introduces a novel noise identiﬁ-
cation mechanism and a beneﬁcial noise-guided optimization strategy 
based on granular-ball representation.
(2) Building on granular-ball representation, we design two com-
plementary indicators that capture deviation at the ball level and con-
sistency at the sample level, thereby constructing a multi-level noise 
sample selection strategy. Based on the identiﬁed noise types, we fur-
ther develop a beneﬁcial noise-guided optimization scheme that jointly 
leverages OOD Dispersion Loss, Prototype Softmax Loss, and Prototype 
Margin Loss to enhance representation learning.
(3) We conduct extensive experiments across multiple datasets and 
noise conﬁgurations, demonstrating clear improvements over represen-
tative baselines in noise identiﬁcation and open intent classiﬁcation. The 
results verify the eﬀectiveness and generality of the proposed approach.
2.  Related work
2.1.  Learning with noisy labels
Learning with noisy labels is fundamental in robust deep learning. 
Existing studies can be grouped into four major categories. Sample se-
lection methods [16,17], which identify diﬀerent noise types based on 
heuristics such as small-loss criterion or consistency across views, and 
use this information to guide robust training. These methods exhibit 
complementary strengths under diﬀerent noise conditions. Label correc-
tion methods [18,19], which attempt to directly revise incorrect labels, 
either via model predictions or auxiliary estimation strategies. Loss cor-
rection methods [20,21], which design robust objective functions that 
are less sensitive to noisy annotations and stabilize the optimization pro-
cess. Transition matrix-based methods [22,23], which aim to explicitly 
model the noise generation process by estimating the label transition 
probabilities and correcting posterior predictions accordingly.
Recent studies highlight the importance of handling both IND noise 
and OOD noise in open-world scenarios. Xia et al. [24] design an ex-
tended 𝑇-estimator to model mixed noise through a cluster-dependent 
transition matrix. Zhang et al. [6] propose a multi-prototype framework 
that separates diﬀerent types of noisy samples via prototype-sample dis-
tances. In addition, recent work shows that controlled noise can ben-
eﬁt diverse modalities. For instance, incentive noise improves vision-
language alignment [25], learned graph noise enhances contrastive 
augmentation [26], frequency-guided variation beneﬁts image gener-
ation [27], initialization-based modulation preserves pretrained knowl-
edge in diﬀusion transformers [28], and facial adversarial noise supports 
privacy-preserving portrait synthesis [29].
Despite recent progress, most existing noise detection methods rely 
on single-aspect cues for noise identiﬁcation and seldom incorporate 
neighborhood information, which limits their ability to distinguish IND 
and OOD noise. In this work, we propose to identify noisy samples by 
constructing multi-perspective indicators and treat OOD noise as a ben-
eﬁcial signal to improve representation.
2.2.  Open intent classiﬁcation
Open Intent Classiﬁcation [30,31] aims to classify intents belonging 
to predeﬁned intent classes while detecting open (unknown) intents. 
This setting is critical in real-world dialogue systems, where new user 
intents frequently emerge. Compared with closed-set classiﬁcation, it 
requires both discriminative modeling of known intents and robust de-
tection of unknowns.
Existing open intent classiﬁcation approaches can be broadly 
grouped into two categories. The ﬁrst is post-hoc unknown detec-
tion, which builds OOD detection mechanisms upon pretrained or

that compute conﬁdence scores from output logits, such as OLT [32], 
which calibrates sparse subnetworks for improved detection; and (2) 
distance-based methods, such as using learned class-wise radii to detect
unknowns [1]. The second is learning discriminative representations for 
OOD detection, which aims to optimize the feature space to separate 
known and unknown intents. For instance, DeepUnk [33] introduces a 
margin loss to enlarge inter-class gaps and reduce intra-class variance. 
Additionally, some methods utilize pseudo-OOD samples to guide repre-
sentation learning; for example, K+1-way [34] constructs pseudo out-
liers to train a discriminative classiﬁer.
Despite recent progress, most methods assume clean training data 
and overlook label noise, which is common in large-scale intent datasets. 
Although a few works in computer vision have explored open-node 
recognition under label noise [2], they remain limited to the image 
domain. Existing studies have rarely addressed the coexistence of IND 
and OOD noise in open intent classiﬁcation. This work ﬁlls the gap by 
proposing a uniﬁed framework that identiﬁes multiple noise types and 
exploits OOD noise to improve open-space representation learning.
2.3.  Granular-ball computing
Granular-ball computing was ﬁrst practically implemented by Xia et 
al. [14] as an eﬃcient and interpretable method for multi-granularity 
data representation. Unlike traditional point-based data, it employs 
spherical structures of varying sizes to adaptively partition and cover the 
data space, thereby improving expressive capacity, eﬃciency, and ro-
bustness when handling complex data. This paradigm has been applied 
in various domains, including granular-ball clustering [15], granular-
ball classiﬁcation [35], granular-ball sampling [36], and others.
Owing to its coarse-grained and robust representations, granular-ball 
computing has recently been explored for addressing noise-related chal-
lenges. For example, Wang et al. [37] applied granular-ball mechanisms 
to adversarial text defense, mitigating the impact of input perturbations. 
Wang et al. [38] utilized granular-balls to ﬁlter noisy labels and enhance 
model generalization.
While these studies demonstrate the potential of granular-ball com-
puting under noisy conditions, they mostly rely on basic granular-ball 
properties for coarse ﬁltering and focus solely on IND noise. In contrast, 
we propose to design multi-perspective indicators based on granular-
ball representations for identifying both IND and OOD noise, aiming to 
enhance open intent classiﬁcation under noisy scenarios.

4.  Methodology
As shown in Fig. 2, the proposed BNO-GB framework consists of three 
main modules. First, we perform unsupervised granular-ball clustering 
over the extracted features to approximate the underlying data distribu-
tion with adaptive and noise-tolerant local structures. Then, we design 
a multi-level noise identiﬁcation strategy by combining two comple-
mentary indicators: a global granular-ball-level indicator to assess the 
outlier tendency (G-ODT), and a local sample-level indicator to evaluate 
inlier consistency (S-ICD). Based on these indicators, samples are cate-
gorized into clean, IND noise, OOD noise, and uncertain types. Finally, 
we introduce a beneﬁcial noise-guided representation learning module, 
where three tailored losses are applied to guide OOD samples away from 
known-class prototypes, aggregate clean and corrected IND samples to-
ward their prototypes, and enforce margins between class prototypes 
to enhance discrimination. In inference, we use multi-granularity de-
cision boundaries for each class to classify known classes and identify 
unknown.
4.1.  Granular-ball-based space approximation
Discovering the neighborhood information and the latent class struc-
ture from noisy data is essential for reliable noise identiﬁcation. Prior 
works have adopted clustering-based approaches to estimate multiple 
prototypes per class to assist in detecting label noise [6]. However, these 
methods typically require a predeﬁned number of clusters for each class 
and often rely on supervised clustering guided by noisy labels, which 
can degrade clustering performance. To address this issue, we propose 
to approximate the underlying representation space using unsupervised 
granular-ball clustering [15], which avoids reliance on noisy labels and 
adaptively ﬁts the data distribution. Compared with conventional clus-
tering methods, granular-ball clustering captures local density, region 
coverage, and structural continuity, making it more eﬀective in reﬂect-
ing the spatial structure of data. The resulting properties of granular-ball 
provide more depictions of data distribution, oﬀering a stronger foun-
dation for downstream noise detection.
Given a dataset 𝐷, we feed the input samples into a pre-trained BERT 
model [39] to extract feature representations 𝑍= {(𝑧𝑖, 𝑦𝑖)}𝑁
𝑖=1. These 
representations are then clustered in an unsupervised manner to form a 
set of granular-balls. The granular-ball clustering process consists of two 
stages: ball generation and ball merging. The overall process is detailed 
as follows.

4.3.  Beneﬁcial noise-guided representation learning
The beneﬁcial role of noise has been demonstrated in many recent 
studies. In the context of open intent classiﬁcation, OOD noise provides 
informative signals that go beyond clean and IND samples, motivating 
us to regard it as a beneﬁcial source and design a beneﬁcial-noise-guided 
representation learning strategy. Based on the identiﬁed clean samples, 
IND noise, and OOD noise, together with the multi-prototype represen-
tations of known classes, we introduce three complementary losses to 
enhance discrimination among known intents and improve robustness 
to unseen ones.

4.4.  Inference strategy
 To perform open intent classiﬁcation during inference, we adopt a 
multi-granularity classiﬁer that builds upon the granular-ball structures 
constructed in the representation space [40]. For each known class, we 
retain its granular-balls with high purity and size (𝑝> 𝑝𝑡, 𝑛> 𝑛𝑡) to rep-
resent its class region, each deﬁned by a centroid and a corresponding 
mean radius. These granular-balls serve as ﬂexible decision regions that 
reﬂect the intrinsic distribution of each class. Given a query representa-
tion, we determine whether it belongs to any known class by checking 
its distance relative to the centroids of all retained granular-balls. If the 
query falls outside the radius of every granular-ball, it is considered an 
unknown sample and assigned to the unknown class. Otherwise, it is 
classiﬁed into the class of the closest granular-ball that covers it. This 
localized, prototype-based decision strategy enables the model to more 
accurately distinguish known intents while eﬀectively rejecting open-
space unknowns.
4.5.  Time complexity analysis
The granular-ball generation module in BNO-GB follows the splitting 
and merging strategy used in MGNR [15]. During the splitting stage, 
each granular-ball is recursively divided until the purity and size con-
straints are satisﬁed. The most time-consuming operation is the iterative 
determination of ball centers by repeatedly identifying farthest points, 
which requires 𝑂(𝑁) time per iteration. Since the maximum number of 
iterations is log 𝑁, the overall time complexity of the splitting stage is 
𝑂(𝑁log 𝑁). In the merging stage, the algorithm evaluates pairwise simi-
larities among the generated granular-balls and performs iterative merg-
ing operations. Let 𝑀 denote the number of granular-balls after split-
ting, typically with 𝑀≪𝑁; consequently, the merging process takes 
𝑂(𝑀log 𝑀) time.
5.  Experiments
In this section, we empirically investigate the open intent classiﬁca-
tion performance of our proposed BNO-GB method in dealing with IND 
noise and OOD noise. In the following, we describe the experimental set-
tings (Section 5.1), experimental results (Section 5.2), ablation studies 
(Section 5.3), analysis of the G-ODT and S-ICD indicators (Section 5.4), 
impact of key parameters during inference (Section 5.5), and computa-
tional cost analysis (Section 5.6).
5.1.  Experimental setup
5.1.1.  Datasets
To comprehensively assess the eﬀectiveness of BNO-GB across di-
verse intent classiﬁcation scenarios, we experiment on three repre-
sentative text datasets commonly used in open intent classiﬁcation.
SNIPS [41] is a lightweight dataset for voice assistant intent recog-
nition, containing 7 intent classes with concise user queries. Stack-
Overﬂow [42] is a multi-domain dataset with 20 technical intent 
classes, drawn from developer Q&A posts with diverse linguistic pat-
terns. BANKING [43] is a domain-speciﬁc dataset covering 77 banking-
related intent classes, featuring ﬁne-grained and formal customer ser-
vice queries. An overview of the datasets is given below, with detailed 
statistics summarized in Table 1. For each dataset, we introduce con-
trolled noise to simulate real-world challenges, with details of the noise 
setting shown in (Section 5.1.2).
5.1.2.  Open and noise setting
We follow classical open intent classiﬁcation settings [1] by ran-
domly selecting a ﬁxed proportion of classes as known classes for train-
ing. The remaining classes of the dataset are treated as unknown classes 
and are used only during testing. The training set contains clean samples, 
IND noise, and OOD noise. All training samples are assigned labels ex-
clusively from the known class set. Speciﬁcally, IND noise is introduced 
by corrupting a portion of known-class samples through random misla-
beling within the known classes. OOD noise is generated by sampling 
data from external out-of-distribution datasets and incorrectly labeling

5.1.3.  Comparison methods
To evaluate the performance of BNO-GB, we compare it with three 
categories of baseline methods. The ﬁrst category includes open intent 
classiﬁcation methods, which aim to detect unknown intents while ac-
curately classifying known ones. Speciﬁcally, we compare with Deep-
Unk (2019) [33], K+1-way (2021) [34], DETER (2024) [44], and OLT
(2024) [32]. The second category is granular-ball-based noise-robust 
classiﬁcation methods. We adopt GBRAIN (2024) [38] as a represen-
tative baseline. Since it lacks the ability to detect unknown intents, 
we incorporate an adaptive decision boundary [1] to enable open in-
tent identiﬁcation. The third category includes Large Language Model 
(LLM) baselines, where we adopt Qwen2-7B-Instruct and Baichuan2-
7B-Chat for open intent classiﬁcation. All methods are evaluated using 
four metrics consistent with prior work [33], including overall Accu-
racy (Acc), macro F1-score across all classes (F1-All), macro F1-score 
over known classes (Known), and macro F1-score over the open class 
(Open). These metrics oﬀer a comprehensive assessment of both gen-
eral and ﬁne-grained performance.
5.1.4.  Implementation details
We use a pre-trained BERT model [39], where all parameters are 
frozen except for the ﬁnal classiﬁcation layer. Training is conducted 
with a batch size of 128 and an initial learning rate of 2e-5. The train-
ing process consists of 10 warm-up epochs, followed by noise recogni-
tion and beneﬁcial noise learning. The total number of training epochs 
is set to 100, with early stopping applied using a patience of 10. Dur-
ing granular-ball clustering, only granular-balls with sample size greater 
than a threshold 𝑛𝑠𝑝𝑙𝑖𝑡 are split. Based on dataset scale, 𝑛𝑠𝑝𝑙𝑖𝑡 is set to 16 
for StackOverﬂow and BANKING, and 150 for SNIPS. In the multi-level 
noise identiﬁcation module, the number of neighbors for the G-ODT in-
dicator is set to 𝑀= 5, and the consistency neighbor size for G-IND is 
𝑇= 5. To select reliable prototypes, we use centroids of granular-balls 
with purity 𝑝ℎ> 0.7 and sample size 𝑛ℎ> 5 across all datasets. For noise 
type classiﬁcation (Eq. (8)), the threshold 𝜃𝑔 is uniformly set to 0.1, 
while 𝜃𝑠 is set to 0.25 for BANKING and StackOverﬂow, and 0.35 for 
SNIPS. In the beneﬁcial noise learning stage, three loss functions are 
jointly optimized: OOD Dispersion Loss 𝑑𝑖𝑠𝑝 (Eq. (9)) with 𝑀𝑜= 5 and 
𝜏= 6.0; Prototype Softmax Loss 𝑝𝑟𝑜𝑡𝑜 (Eq. 12); and Prototype Margin 
Loss 𝑚𝑎𝑟𝑔𝑖𝑛 (Eq. (14)) with margin 𝛿= 0.5. The weights of these losses 
are set to 𝛼= 1.0, 𝛽= 1.0, and 𝛾= 1.0, respectively.
During inference, decision boundaries are constructed using the cen-
troids and radii of granular-balls with purity above 𝑝𝑡 and sample size 
above 𝑛𝑡. Speciﬁcally, we set 𝑝𝑡= 0.9 when the training noise ratio is 
0.2, and 𝑝𝑡= 0.8 when the noise ratio is 0.4. The value of 𝑛𝑡 is dataset-
dependent.
5.2.  Experimental results
5.2.1.  Main results
Table 2 presents the F1-score and Acc of BNO-GB and other base-
lines on the SNIPS, StackOverﬂow, and BANKING datasets. Each value 
represents the average performance over four runs with diﬀerent ran-
dom seeds. The experiments are conducted under two known-class ratios 
(25% and 50%) and two noise levels (20% and 40%). The best results 
among all methods are highlighted in bold, while the second-best re-
sults are marked with underline. From Table 2, we observe that when 
the noise level increases from 20% to 40%, both the F1-score and Acc 
of BNO-GB decrease on almost all datasets and settings. This is because 
a higher noise ratio makes it more challenging to accurately identify 
noisy samples and to learn stable intent representations. Table 3 presents 
ﬁne-grained F1-scores for known and open classes across the SNIPS, 
StackOverﬂow, and BANKING datasets under diﬀerent combinations of 
known-class ratios (25% and 50%) and noise levels (20% and 40%). 
From Table 3, we observe that for BNO-GB, increasing the known-class 
ratio from 25% to 50% generally leads to higher F1-scores on known 
classes but lower F1-scores on open classes. This phenomenon can be 
explained by the fact that a larger known-class ratio provides richer su-
pervision and clearer intra-class structure for distinguishing known in-
tents, which improves the F1-score on known classes. However, it also 
reduces the relative size of the open space, causing unseen intents to 
overlap more with known regions and making open-class detection more 
diﬃcult, which leads to lower F1-scores on open classes.
By jointly examining Tables 2 and 3, we can see that BNO-GB 
achieves the best or highly competitive performance across diﬀerent 
datasets, noise ratios, and known-class ratios, and outperforms all base-
line methods. These improvements mainly stem from two key compo-
nents of our framework. First, the granular-ball-based multi-level noise 
identiﬁcation enables more reliable separation of clean samples, IND 
noise, and OOD noise, which allows the model to learn from structurally 
trustworthy samples even in the presence of severe label noise. Second, 
the beneﬁcial noise-guided learning scheme explicitly leverages OOD 
noise to shape the open region and reinforces the separation between 
known and unknown intents. The combination of these two components 
leads to more discriminative representations and more accurate open in-
tent detection.
In addition, we observe that the LLM-based Qwen2-7B-Instruct 
achieves relatively good performance on the SNIPS and StackOverﬂow 
datasets, where several metrics reach the second-best level. However, 
its performance degrades signiﬁcantly on the BANKING dataset, which 
suggests that current large models still face challenges when dealing 
with tasks involving a larger number of intent categories. We also ﬁnd 
that Baichuan2-7B-Chat performs much worse than Qwen2-7B-Instruct 
under almost all settings. Overall, BNO-GB surpasses both LLM-based 
baselines, which further demonstrates the eﬀectiveness and robustness 
of the proposed method.

5.3.2.  Assessment of key components
Our proposed method introduces two core innovations: (1) a multi-
level noise identiﬁcation strategy based on the G-ODT and S-ICD in-
dicators, and (2) a beneﬁcial noise learning strategy with tailored loss 
functions. To evaluate the individual contributions of these components, 
we implement and test the following variants of our model. BNO-GB: 
The full model with multi-level noise identiﬁcation (G-ODT and S-ICD) 
and beneﬁcial noise learning using all three loss functions. w/o G-ODT 
& S-ICD: a variant with noise identiﬁcation is removed. Training is per-
formed on the full noisy dataset using standard softmax loss, and in-
ference still adopts granular-ball-based decision boundaries. w/o 𝑑𝑖𝑠𝑝: 
a variant with OOD Dispersion Loss is removed. w/o 𝑝𝑟𝑜𝑡𝑜: a variant 
with Prototype Softmax Loss is removed. w/o 𝑚𝑎𝑟𝑔𝑖𝑛: a variant with 
Prototype Margin Loss is removed.
Table 6 presents the performance of all ablation variants on Stack-
Overﬂow and SNIPS under the 25% known class ratio and 20% noise 
setting. Experiments on the same dataset are conducted using the same 
hyperparameter conﬁguration, and results are averaged over four dif-
ferent random seeds for robustness. As shown in the Table 6, removing 
any single component results in a performance drop, demonstrating that 
each module makes a meaningful contribution to the overall eﬀective-
ness of BNO-GB.
5.4.  Analysis of G-ODT and S-ICD
In Section 4.2, we proposed two indicators, G-ODT and S-ICD, and 
used their values along with label information to make noise recogni-
tion. To assess the discriminative capability of the proposed indicators, 
we plot the probability density distributions of G-ODT and S-ICD values 
for clean samples, IND noise, and OOD noise, categorized according to 
ground-truth labels on the StackOverﬂow and SNIPS datasets, as shown 
in Fig. 3 (a)-(d).
Fig. 3(a) and (c) present the distribution of G-ODT values. It can 
be observed that the G-ODT values of clean and IND noise samples 
are primarily concentrated near zero, indicating that their correspond-
ing granular-balls maintain label consistency with neighboring balls 
and are positioned near the same-label balls in the feature space. In 
contrast, the G-ODT values of OOD noise samples tend to be higher, 
suggesting that their granular-balls deviate signiﬁcantly from known 
classes. These results conﬁrm the eﬀectiveness of the G-ODT indica-
tor in capturing out-of-distribution tendencies. Fig. 3(b) and (d) show 
the S-ICD value distributions. Across both datasets, clean and IND noise 
samples share similar distributions, with relatively high S-ICD values 
concentrated on the right-hand side, whereas OOD noise samples ex-
hibit signiﬁcantly lower S-ICD values concentrated in the left-hand re-
gion. This indicates that the S-ICD indicator eﬀectively captures the 
in-distribution consistency of samples, allowing for reliable noise-type
diﬀerentiation.
In summary, G-ODT and S-ICD provide complementary perspectives 
at the granular-ball level and the sample level, respectively, for mod-
eling outlier and inlier tendencies. Their distribution patterns not only 
validate the discriminative ability of each individual indicator but also 
demonstrate their synergistic potential in jointly enabling robust noise 
identiﬁcation under open-world conditions.

class ratio of 25% and a total noise ratio of 40%. Fig. 4(a)–(d) illus-

in increments of 0.1, under diﬀerent ﬁxed values of 𝑛𝑡 set to 8, 10, 12, 
and 14, respectively. The plots show the eﬀects of 𝑝𝑡 on four evaluation 
metrics: Known, Open, F1-All, and Acc.
The results reveal a consistent pattern, as the purity threshold in-
creases, all performance metrics initially improve, indicating that ex-
cluding low-purity granular-balls enhances the reliability and discrim-
inative ability of the decision boundary. However, when 𝑝𝑡 becomes 
too large (e.g., 𝑝𝑡= 0.9), a noticeable performance drop occurs in cer-
tain settings, particularly in subﬁgure (d), with the Known and F1-score 
metrics exhibiting sharp declines. This suggests that overly strict pu-
rity constraints may result in insuﬃcient sample coverage, leading to 
the exclusion of informative data during training. Moreover, as the size 
threshold 𝑛𝑡 increases, the peak performance tends to shift toward lower 
purity values, indicating that when the granular-ball size requirement 
becomes stricter, the model relies more on medium-purity balls for eﬀec-
tive generalization. It is also worth noting that across all subﬁgures, the 
performance on unknowns (Open) is mostly the highest. This highlights 
the eﬀectiveness of our Beneﬁcial Noise-guided Representation Learn-
ing module in promoting open space representation, thereby enhancing 
the model’s ability to recognize open intents.

6.  Conclusions
In this paper, we present a novel framework, BNO-GB, to tackle 
open intent classiﬁcation in the presence of both IND and OOD noisy 
labels. Speciﬁcally, we perform granular-ball clustering to obtain noise-
robust granular-ball representations. In addition, we design a multi-
level noise sample selection strategy by combining granular-ball-level 
and sample-level indicators to accurately identify clean, IND noise, and 
OOD noise samples. Furthermore, we develop a beneﬁcial noise-guided 
learning strategy that leverages OOD noise to expand the open space, 
while jointly enhancing class representation and inter-class separabil-
ity through three tailored loss functions. Extensive experiments demon-
strate the eﬀectiveness of our method across various noise scenarios. Al-
though BNO-GB exhibits strong robustness under complex noise, several 
parameters, including the granular-ball thresholds used in splitting and 
inference, remain sensitive to the scale of the dataset. This introduces 
limited manual conﬁguration when adapting to datasets of diﬀerent den-
sities. In future work, we plan to develop adaptive or parameter-free 
granular-ball mechanisms to automatically determine these thresholds. 
We also aim to further improve computational eﬃciency and extend the 
framework to broader open intent understanding scenarios.

content.text:
你的直觉是**对的,而且这是一个能救命的发现**。如果不读这篇原文就去写 idea,新方向开局就会撞墙。我把残酷的真相说清楚。

## 你的 idea ≈ BNO-GB,撞车程度高到危险

我把我交接文件里写的 idea 和 BNO-GB 的实际算法逐条对齐:

| 我的 idea(交接文件 §3.1) | BNO-GB 实际做了什么 | 撞车? |
|---|---|---|
| 在 BERT embedding 上建多粒度粒球 | §4.1 BERT(frozen)+ 无监督粒球聚类(splitting+merging) | **完全相同** |
| 球带 中心/半径/密度/纯度 | §3.1 centroid/radius/purity 全有 | **完全相同** |
| 球间重叠度 = 模糊边界 | §4.1.2 ball merging 用球间重叠 `‖o_i−o_j‖−(r_i+r_j)<φ` | **相同** |
| 球间一致性 / 邻居球标签 | §4.2.1 **G-ODT** = 到 M 个同标签近邻球距离 × T 个近邻球标签不一致率 | **相同** |
| 样本到球心归属强度(半径归一化) | §4.2.2 **S-ICD** = `purity × exp(−‖z−o‖/r)` | **几乎逐字相同** |
| 未知拒识 = 落在大半径/球外 | §4.4 inference:query 落在所有球半径外 → unknown,否则归最近覆盖球的类 | **相同** |
| 评测 AUROC/unknown-F1/macro-F1 | §5 用 Acc/F1-All/Known/Open,4 seeds | **相同协议** |
| 数据集 CLINC/BANKING/SNIPS | SNIPS/StackOverflow/**BANKING** | **重叠** |

**结论:我交接文件里的"主方法 DGB-OB",有 90% 是 BNO-GB 已经发表(Pattern Recognition 2026,有开源代码 github.com/Liyanhuaa/BNO_GB)的东西。** S-ICD 那个公式 `p_j·exp(−‖z−o‖/r)` 和我说的"用半径密度归一化的归属强度"是同一个东西。我之前把 BNO-GB 当"可借鉴的相关工作",**严重低估了它——它不是相关工作,它就是我提的方法本身。** 这是我的失误,幸好你的直觉拦住了。

## 但坏消息里有一个真正的好消息——BNO-GB 暴露了它自己的两个缺口

读原文时我盯着它**没做什么、自己承认的局限**,这才是你的真空位:

1. **BNO-GB 全程是"静态后处理"——和你失败的 SoftDist 同一个架构病。** 它 BERT 冻结(只训最后一层),球建一次、算 G-ODT/S-ICD 一次、选样一次,然后训练三个 prototype loss。**球不参与表示的动态演化。** 它甚至在 §6 Conclusion 亲口说局限是"球的阈值(splitting/inference)对数据集尺度敏感,需要手工配"。
2. **BNO-GB 的拒识完全靠 prototype 距离 + 球覆盖**——这正是 OOD 领域最标准的 prototype-distance 打分。**它从没证明过它的球信号对"标准 OOD 打分(MSP/Energy/Mahalanobis/kNN-OOD)"有条件增益**——也就是说,BNO-GB 自己**没过我们那个第一闸门**!它只对标了 DeepUnk/K+1-way/GBAIN,**没对标任何一个标准 post-hoc OOD 打分**。

## 所以方向要调整——这是关键判断

**不能再做"BNO-GB 的换皮"**(多粒度粒球边界+G-ODT+S-ICD+prototype loss),那会被审稿人一句"和 BNO-GB(PR 2026)有何区别"毙掉。**真正的空位是 BNO-GB 留下的那两个洞**:

- **洞1(动态化)**:把粒球从 BNO-GB 的"一次性静态选样"变成**训练过程中动态参与**(课程/置信度调度,球随表示演化重建)——这正是我们三方锁定的"角色",而 BNO-GB **恰恰没做**(它冻结 BERT、静态建球)。这是真差异化。
- **洞2(无参)**:BNO-GB 自己承认阈值敏感、要手调——你做**无参/自适应阈值**版本,正好踩在它的 future work 上。

**而第一闸门(条件增益)反而更值钱了**:因为 BNO-GB 自己都没证明球信号 vs 标准 OOD 打分的增益——如果你能证明,你不仅区别于 BNO-GB,还顺手补了它的实验空白。

## 我要诚实纠正交接文件

我之前写的交接文件 §3.1 主方法**有严重撞车风险,必须改**。正确的新定位应该是:

> **不是"用粒球做 open-intent 边界+拒识"(=BNO-GB),而是"让粒球在训练过程中动态调度(课程/置信度),并证明其不确定性信号对标准 OOD 打分有条件增益"——攻击 BNO-GB 的静态架构 + 无参 + 未验证条件增益 三个缺口。**

我现在去快速看一眼另外两篇(G-GBC 的 GMM 椭球、Three-Level 的三层度量),确认它们有没有进一步缩小这个空位,然后把交接文件的 §3 和 deep-research 提示词都改对。

要我现在就:(1) 读完那两篇 → (2) 把交接文件 §3 改成"攻击 BNO-GB 三缺口"的正确定位 + 把 BNO-GB 列为头号竞品(必须切割)→ (3) 重写 deep-research 提示词(加一条:专门查 BNO-GB 之后还有没有人做了动态/无参版本,以及标准 OOD 打分全集作为第一闸门靶子)?

这是防止新方向开局即死的关键修正,我建议立刻做。你同意我就继续。

21	a b s t r a c t
22	In actual scenarios, both manual and automated annotation methods are susceptible to generating mislabeled 
23	data. Existing noise-handling techniques primarily focus on penalizing or eliminating noisy labels; however, they 
24	often face challenges in maintaining interpretability and eﬀectively addressing the complexities of label noise. To 
25	address these issues, we propose a novel framework that leverages the robustness and interpretability of granular-
26	ball computing (GBC) to improve noise resistance and classiﬁcation performance. The Gaussian mixture-based 
27	GBC (G-GBC) method integrates CNN models as a feature extractor and employs a Gaussian mixture model to 
28	adaptively generate granular-ball (GB). By incorporating the purity and weight of GBs into the classiﬁcation 
29	process, the model dynamically adjusts the granularity of GBs, enabling it to extract essential features while 
30	reducing the adverse eﬀects of noise. Experimental results on multiple datasets demonstrate that the proposed 
31	approach signiﬁcantly enhances classiﬁcation accuracy and model robustness under noisy conditions. Further-
32	more, the GB framework improves the interpretability of the training process, oﬀering a novel perspective for 
33	image classiﬁcation tasks in the presence of label noise.
34	1.  Introduction
35	In deep learning applications, the issue of noisy labels has emerged 
36	as a notable challenge, limiting both model robustness and generaliza-
37	tion performance. Noisy labels are prevalent in real-world datasets, re-
38	sulting from various factors such as human annotation errors, random 
39	interference during data collection, and background complexity [1]. In 
40	medical prediction problems, for example, diagnostic labels often suﬀer 
41	from inter- and intra-expert disagreement or are automatically extracted 
42	from clinical text, which leads to label uncertainty and can substan-
43	tially deteriorate the performance and fairness of deep learning models 
44	used for decision support [2]. Similar challenges arise in large-scale in-
45	formation systems that rely on crowdsourcing, where labels provided 
46	by non-expert annotators remain noisy even after aggregation; recent 
47	work shows that explicit label-noise modelling and correction are cru-
48	cial to maintain data quality and downstream model accuracy in such 
49	settings [3,4]. These label inaccuracies disrupt the learning process, of-
50	ten causing models to memorize erroneous information during train-
51	ing and leading to overﬁtting [5]. Consequently, model classiﬁcation 
52	accuracy decreases, and generalization performance signiﬁcantly suf-

58	data augmentation and early stopping [6], partially mitigate the impact 
59	of noise. However, their eﬀectiveness depends on noise intensity and 
60	data distribution complexity, making them insuﬃcient in high-noise or 
61	complex data environments [7].
62	Deep CNNs possess an inherent capacity to ﬁt both clean and noisy 
63	data, which means that they are likely to memorize incorrect labels in 
64	the presence of label noise, leading to overﬁtting and reduced general-
65	ization performance [8]. This phenomenon becomes more pronounced 
66	in deeper models, as they tend to exhibit higher expressive power and 
67	thus adapt more readily to noise. In addition, label noise disrupts the 
68	hierarchical feature extraction process of CNNs, particularly in early 
69	layers, which can propagate errors to subsequent layers, compounding 
70	the negative eﬀects [9]. To address the issue of noisy labels, numer-
71	ous classical and reﬁned strategies have been developed in recent years. 
72	For instance, loss-based noisy sample detection methods use sample loss 
73	to distinguish noisy data [10]; adversarial training methods introduce 
74	adversarial samples to enhance model robustness [11]; and robust loss 
75	functions [12,13] are widely adopted to reduce sensitivity to outlier la-
76	bels. Although these methods are eﬀective in handling certain levels

89	Despite the progress made, notable research gaps remain. First, many 
90	approaches rely on assumptions or estimations about noise distribution 
91	to set appropriate parameters, which can be particularly challenging in 
92	real-world datasets where noise arises from complex and unpredictable 
93	sources [14]. For instance, some methods assume a ﬁxed proportion 
94	of noisy labels or require an estimate of noise rates, which may not 
95	hold in varied or dynamic environments [15]. These assumptions limit 
96	the generalizability of such methods in diverse datasets with heteroge-
97	neous noise types and levels [16]. Second, most existing methods are 
98	computationally intensive, hindering their scalability to large datasets, 
99	particularly within the high-dimensional feature spaces of deep learn-
100	ing. For example, methods such as label smoothing or sample reweight-
101	ing often require additional computational resources for each epoch, 
102	hindering their application in real-time or resource-constrained settings 
103	[17,18]. As the size and complexity of deep learning applications con-
104	tinue to grow, the demand for methods that can maintain both accuracy 
105	and computational eﬃciency becomes increasingly critical. Lastly, ex-
106	isting methods primarily focus on adjusting loss functions or prescreen-
107	ing samples without adaptively balancing noise and useful information 
108	from a multi-granular perspective [19]. Noise-robust learning strategies 
109	are often designed almost exclusively with predictive performance in 
110	mind and oﬀer limited interpretability regarding how models behave 
111	under conﬂicting or corrupted labels. However, in high-impact or reg-
112	ulated applications, interpretability is a key requirement for deploying 
113	noise-robust models, since stakeholders need to understand and scruti-
114	nize model behaviour under noisy supervision in order to establish trust 
115	and ensure responsible use.
116	Against this background, granular-ball computing (GBC) introduces 
117	an innovative multi-granularity processing mechanism that is promising 
118	for both robustness and interpretability [20]. Its theoretical foundation 
119	can be traced to information granulation theories such as fuzzy sets and 
120	rough sets [21], which structure data hierarchically for graded informa-
121	tion processing. However, these theories are generally applied to simpler 
122	structures. GBC employs granular-ball (GB) of varying granularity to 
123	achieve multilevel data segmentation, enabling the model to make clas-
124	siﬁcation decisions across multiple granularity levels [22]. Unlike tradi-
125	tional methods, GBC dynamically adjusts the granularity size, adaptively 
126	extracting information at diﬀerent levels based on data distribution. 
127	This multilayered processing capability allows the model to disregard 
128	noise at coarser granularity levels while capturing valuable informa-
129	tion at ﬁner levels, thereby achieving robust and stable performance on 
130	noisy datasets [23]. However, existing GBC-based methods, such as the 
131	Granular-Ball Support Vector Machine (GBSVM) [24], primarily focus 
132	on enhancing the eﬃciency of traditional classiﬁers by replacing ﬁne-
133	grained samples with GBs. Unfortunately, these methods often rely on 
134	rigid clustering techniques, such as the K-means method. This reliance 
135	limits their ability to handle multimodal or irregularly shaped data dis-
136	tributions, as the K-means method assumes spherical clusters and equal 
137	variances, leading to suboptimal granularity adaptation in complex, 
138	high-dimensional, noisy environments. Furthermore, these methods are 
139	typically designed for shallow machine learning paradigms and lack 
140	seamless integration with deep learning architectures, such as CNNs, 
141	resulting in limited ﬂexibility for noise probabilistic modeling and in-
142	suﬃcient empirical gains in classiﬁcation accuracy under severe label 
143	noise.
144	To address these limitations and ﬁll the identiﬁed research gaps, 
145	this study introduces Gaussian Mixture-Based granular-ball computing 
146	(G-GBC) method that integrates GBC with Gaussian Mixture Models 
147	(GMM) optimized by Mahalanobis distance. This provides a new ap-
148	proach that leverages the robustness of granular balls and the soft as-
149	signment mechanism of GMM from a multi-granularity perspective to 
150	improve the robustness of GBC-based methods in noisy environments. 
151	G-GBC enhances multi-granularity processing by incorporating proba-
152	bilistic soft assignments from GMM, which allow for dynamic purity-
153	weighted adjustments and better preservation of data structures in noisy 
154	settings. By dynamically adjusting GB granularity and leveraging purity-
155	weighted assignments, the proposed approach mitigates the impact of 
156	label noise while preserving critical data structures. The integration of 
157	this method into CNNs not only improves performance on high-noise 
158	datasets but also provides enhanced interpretability through visualizing 
159	the evolution of GB structures during training. These contributions pro-
160	vide a practical approach to improving robustness and interpretability 
161	in deep learning models. The main contributions of this paper are as 
162	follows:
163	1. We present a novel method to address the challenges associated 
164	with noisy labels. The proposed method leverages the adaptive clus-
165	tering capability of GBs to mitigate the adverse eﬀects of misla-
166	beled data. By dynamically adjusting the GB formation process and 
167	incorporating noise-tolerant mechanisms, the proposed method ef-
168	fectively reduces the impact of label noise, enhancing classiﬁcation 
169	accuracy and robustness in high-noise environments.
170	2. The proposed adaptive Gaussian mixture-based GBC (G-GBC) 
171	method uses a Gaussian mixture model (GMM) with Mahalanobis 
172	distance optimization to accurately capture data distributions. By 
173	dynamically adjusting the granularity and weight of GBs, the pro-
174	posed method eﬀectively mitigates the impact of label noise. This 
175	design enhances the noise resilience of the representation, improv-
176	ing clustering performance and feature extraction accuracy on high-
177	noise datasets.
178	3. The G-GBC method integrates into a CNN framework, enhancing 
179	both robustness and interpretability. This integration leverages the 
180	noise-resilient properties of GBs alongside the powerful feature ex-
181	traction capabilities of CNNs, considerably improving performance 
182	on noisy datasets. Furthermore, the dynamic visualization of GB 
183	evolution elucidates the model’s adaptive mechanisms, enhancing 
184	transparency and interpretability during the training process.
185	2.  Related work
186	2.1.  Granular-ball computing
187	A previous study [25] highlighted that human cognition prioritizes 
188	the recognition of “broad” contour information in images, introducing 
189	the concept of “global precedence.” This perspective diﬀers from most 
190	AI algorithms that rely on ﬁne-grained data points. Building on the abil-
191	ity of granular computing to partition data and knowledge spaces, Wang 
192	[26] proposed multi-granular cognitive computing, while Xia et al. [20] 
193	introduced the idea of using hyperspheres to represent “grains,” lead-
194	ing to the development of GBC. Further advances, such as the GBSVM 
195	[24], demonstrated that GBC can enhance eﬃciency and robustness by 
196	replacing the ﬁnest-grained samples with GBs.
197	GBC extends this concept by adapting data representation into multi-
198	granularity GBs, which serve as multi-scale, adaptive units that enclose 
199	portions of the sample space. Unlike traditional ﬁne-grained methods 
200	that rely on individual data points or small clusters, GBC leverages 
201	larger, coarser GBs to capture the essential structure of the data while 
202	ﬁltering out noise. This allows for more eﬃcient data processing and 
203	enhanced robustness, as GBC can focus on signiﬁcant patterns at vari-
204	ous levels granularity, rather than being disrupted by minute variations 
205	in noisy datasets [27].

277	2.2.  Learning with noisy labels
278	The handling of noisy labels has garnered substantial attention in 
279	recent years, with researchers proposing various eﬀective strategies to 
280	mitigate the disruptive eﬀects of noise on deep learning models, thereby 
281	enhancing model robustness and accuracy. Based on the characteris-
282	tics of these approaches, we classify them into two main categories: 
283	methods focused on label reﬁnement and robust optimization, which 
284	directly address noisy labels through correction, robust loss designs, or 
285	meta-learning techniques; and methods centered on training strategies 
286	and regularization, which leverage training dynamics and regularization 
287	techniques to prevent overﬁtting to noise.
288	2.2.1.  Label reﬁnement and robust optimization methods
289	These methods focus on improving label quality and optimizing the 
290	learning process to minimize the impact of noise. Lee et al. [33] pro-
291	posed CleanNet, a transfer learning framework for scalable image clas-
292	siﬁer training under label noise, enabling eﬃcient correction through 
293	prototype-based veriﬁcation. Huang et al. [34] introduced contrastive 
294	label correction, which enhances noisy label learning by leveraging con-
295	trastive learning to reﬁne labels based on feature similarities. Tu et al. 
296	[35] presented a decoupled meta label puriﬁer, separating label puriﬁ-
297	cation from model training to eﬀectively learn from noisy labels while 
298	avoiding interference. Liu and Guo [36] introduced peer loss functions, 
299	enabling eﬀective learning from noisy labels without requiring prior 
300	knowledge of noise rates by comparing predictions across samples. Wei 
301	et al. [37] proposed co-regularization within a joint training framework, 
302	which inherently provides robustness through agreement-based losses.

307	2.2.2.  Training strategies and regularization methods
308	These methods stabilize the training process and exploit dynamics 
309	to avoid memorizing noisy labels. Tanaka et al. [38] proposed a joint 
310	optimization framework for learning with noisy labels, combining la-
311	bel correction with regularization to improve robustness. Liu et al. [39] 
312	proposed early-learning regularization, which prevents the memoriza-
313	tion of noisy labels by intervening in the initial training phases. Li et al. 
314	[40] introduced DivideMix, which treats noisy label learning as semi-
315	supervised by dividing data into clean and noisy sets for adapted train-
316	ing. Bai et al. [41] investigated and improved early stopping strategies 
317	for learning with noisy labels, optimizing termination points to maxi-
318	mize robustness.
319	2.2.3.  Granular ball computing methods for noisy label learning
320	GBC has emerged as a promising paradigm for addressing noisy la-
321	bels, leveraging its inherent robustness, scalability, and adaptive granu-
322	larity to mitigate the eﬀects of noise in classiﬁcation tasks. Xia et al. [42] 
323	proposed GB sampling (GBS), which adaptively covers the data space 
324	with hyperballs to reduce data size while ﬁltering noisy labels, achiev-
325	ing higher accuracy than random sampling in noisy and imbalanced 
326	classiﬁcation. Qian et al. [43] introduced a granularity tuning approach 
327	for generalized GBs, incorporating weight factors and de-overlapping to 
328	remove heterogeneous overlaps, thereby enhancing classiﬁcation per-
329	formance on diverse datasets. Dai et al. [44] developed a GBC module 
330	for CNNs that splits features into GB samples by sharing single labels, 
331	modifying gradients, and using experience replay to improve robustness 
332	without requiring additional data cleaning.
333	3.  Base model and deﬁnition
334	Clustering is a fundamental step in GB generation as it determines 
335	how data points are grouped to form compact and meaningful repre-
336	sentations. Eﬀective clustering methods can directly impact the qual-
337	ity of GBs, inﬂuencing the model’s ability to handle complex and noisy 
338	datasets. Given the variety of clustering algorithms available, selecting 
339	a suitable approach becomes critical, especially when considering the 
340	trade-oﬀ between computational eﬃciency and the ability to capture 
341	intricate data distributions.
342	This section compares K-means and GMM for GB generation, high-
343	lighting their strengths and limitations in handling complex and noisy 
344	datasets.
345	3.1.  Clustering using K-means
346	In GB generation, selecting an appropriate clustering method is cru-
347	cial. Hard clustering methods, such as K-means, DBSCAN, and spectral 
348	clustering, assign data points deterministically to clusters, which can 
349	limit their eﬀectiveness in complex, noisy environments. These meth-
350	ods are widely used for data partitioning owing to their eﬃciency and 
351	simplicity in certain scenarios. However, they share common limitations 
352	when handling nonspherical, multimodal, or noisy data distributions. 
353	The traditional K-means clustering method is widely used for various 
354	data partitioning tasks because of its eﬃciency and simplicity. How-
355	ever, the K-means clustering method has certain limitations when han-
356	dling complex datasets, particularly in cases involving nonspherical and 
357	multimodal data distributions [45]. Similarly, DBSCAN, a density-based 
358	method, relies on parameters such as minPts and eps to deﬁne clus-
359	ter density, which can lead to instability in high-dimensional or sparse 
360	batch data, often classifying points as noise or failing to form clusters 
361	in small batches [46]. Spectral clustering, which constructs a similarity 
362	graph and performs eigenvalue decomposition, incurs high computa-
363	tional complexity and is better suited for large, well-structured datasets 
364	than for dynamic per-batch processing in noisy, high-dimensional fea-
365	tures [47]. Furthermore, these hard clustering approaches lack prob-
366	abilistic uncertainty modeling, making them sensitive to label noise, 
367	where erroneous points can rigidly inﬂuence cluster boundaries. By con-
368	trast, GMM is a probabilistic density model that better accommodates 
369	multimodal distributions and clusters of varying shapes. When deal-
370	ing with noisy data and high-dimensional datasets, GMM demonstrates 
371	greater ﬂexibility and robustness [48].

578	4.  Method
579	Traditional GB classiﬁers rely on purity judgments and k-means clus-
580	tering, using purity thresholds to determine whether to split or stop 
581	clustering. While eﬀective in handling simple structures, GB classiﬁers 
582	face challenges when dealing with datasets containing a large number 
583	of categories, as their interpretability and clustering power diminish 
584	in complex feature spaces. Conversely, deep learning models optimize 
585	parameters through loss functions to achieve high accuracy; however, 
586	they often lack transparency, making it diﬃcult to interpret their learn-
587	ing process. To address these limitations, we propose G-GBC model that 
588	combines the interpretability of GB classiﬁers with the feature extrac-
589	tion power of deep learning. We present a detailed description of the 
590	proposed approach, including the overall framework and the four key
591	modules.
592	The G-GBC framework integrates GBC into the CNN training pipeline 
593	in an end-to-end manner, with dynamic per-batch adaptation to evolv-
594	ing model representations. In each forward pass (per training batch), 
595	features are extracted from the current batch using the model’s feature 
596	extractor. These batch features serve as input to the adaptive GB genera-
597	tion process, which ﬁts GMM-based granular balls directly on the batch 
598	feature space. The resulting GB parameters (centers, covariances, and 
599	purities) are computed on-the-ﬂy and used immediately for Mahalanobis 
600	similarities and weighted fusions within the same batch, enabling ef-
601	ﬁcient noise-robust classiﬁcation with real-time reﬁnement. This per-
602	batch reﬁtting ensures that GBs dynamically adapt as the feature ex-
603	tractor improves with training, capturing higher-quality, noise-resilient 
604	representations at each step. This integration, as shown in Fig. 3, eﬀec-
605	tively combines deep learning for feature extraction and GB models for 
606	classiﬁcation.

a b s t r a c t
In actual scenarios, both manual and automated annotation methods are susceptible to generating mislabeled 
data. Existing noise-handling techniques primarily focus on penalizing or eliminating noisy labels; however, they 
often face challenges in maintaining interpretability and eﬀectively addressing the complexities of label noise. To 
address these issues, we propose a novel framework that leverages the robustness and interpretability of granular-
ball computing (GBC) to improve noise resistance and classiﬁcation performance. The Gaussian mixture-based 
GBC (G-GBC) method integrates CNN models as a feature extractor and employs a Gaussian mixture model to 
adaptively generate granular-ball (GB). By incorporating the purity and weight of GBs into the classiﬁcation 
process, the model dynamically adjusts the granularity of GBs, enabling it to extract essential features while 
reducing the adverse eﬀects of noise. Experimental results on multiple datasets demonstrate that the proposed 
approach signiﬁcantly enhances classiﬁcation accuracy and model robustness under noisy conditions. Further-
more, the GB framework improves the interpretability of the training process, oﬀering a novel perspective for 
image classiﬁcation tasks in the presence of label noise.
1.  Introduction
In deep learning applications, the issue of noisy labels has emerged 
as a notable challenge, limiting both model robustness and generaliza-
tion performance. Noisy labels are prevalent in real-world datasets, re-
sulting from various factors such as human annotation errors, random 
interference during data collection, and background complexity [1]. In 
medical prediction problems, for example, diagnostic labels often suﬀer 
from inter- and intra-expert disagreement or are automatically extracted 
from clinical text, which leads to label uncertainty and can substan-
tially deteriorate the performance and fairness of deep learning models 
used for decision support [2]. Similar challenges arise in large-scale in-
formation systems that rely on crowdsourcing, where labels provided 
by non-expert annotators remain noisy even after aggregation; recent 
work shows that explicit label-noise modelling and correction are cru-
cial to maintain data quality and downstream model accuracy in such 
settings [3,4]. These label inaccuracies disrupt the learning process, of-
ten causing models to memorize erroneous information during train-
ing and leading to overﬁtting [5]. Consequently, model classiﬁcation 
accuracy decreases, and generalization performance signiﬁcantly suf-

data augmentation and early stopping [6], partially mitigate the impact 
of noise. However, their eﬀectiveness depends on noise intensity and 
data distribution complexity, making them insuﬃcient in high-noise or 
complex data environments [7].
Deep CNNs possess an inherent capacity to ﬁt both clean and noisy 
data, which means that they are likely to memorize incorrect labels in 
the presence of label noise, leading to overﬁtting and reduced general-
ization performance [8]. This phenomenon becomes more pronounced 
in deeper models, as they tend to exhibit higher expressive power and 
thus adapt more readily to noise. In addition, label noise disrupts the 
hierarchical feature extraction process of CNNs, particularly in early 
layers, which can propagate errors to subsequent layers, compounding 
the negative eﬀects [9]. To address the issue of noisy labels, numer-
ous classical and reﬁned strategies have been developed in recent years. 
For instance, loss-based noisy sample detection methods use sample loss 
to distinguish noisy data [10]; adversarial training methods introduce 
adversarial samples to enhance model robustness [11]; and robust loss 
functions [12,13] are widely adopted to reduce sensitivity to outlier la-
bels. Although these methods are eﬀective in handling certain levels

of noise, they often require manual adjustment or rely on prior assump-
tions about noise distribution. This dependency limits their eﬀectiveness 
when facing complex noise distributions or high-noise environments, 
limiting their applicability in large-scale datasets or extreme noise sce-
narios.
Despite the progress made, notable research gaps remain. First, many 
approaches rely on assumptions or estimations about noise distribution 
to set appropriate parameters, which can be particularly challenging in 
real-world datasets where noise arises from complex and unpredictable 
sources [14]. For instance, some methods assume a ﬁxed proportion 
of noisy labels or require an estimate of noise rates, which may not 
hold in varied or dynamic environments [15]. These assumptions limit 
the generalizability of such methods in diverse datasets with heteroge-
neous noise types and levels [16]. Second, most existing methods are 
computationally intensive, hindering their scalability to large datasets, 
particularly within the high-dimensional feature spaces of deep learn-
ing. For example, methods such as label smoothing or sample reweight-
ing often require additional computational resources for each epoch, 
hindering their application in real-time or resource-constrained settings 
[17,18]. As the size and complexity of deep learning applications con-
tinue to grow, the demand for methods that can maintain both accuracy 
and computational eﬃciency becomes increasingly critical. Lastly, ex-
isting methods primarily focus on adjusting loss functions or prescreen-
ing samples without adaptively balancing noise and useful information 
from a multi-granular perspective [19]. Noise-robust learning strategies 
are often designed almost exclusively with predictive performance in 
mind and oﬀer limited interpretability regarding how models behave 
under conﬂicting or corrupted labels. However, in high-impact or reg-
ulated applications, interpretability is a key requirement for deploying 
noise-robust models, since stakeholders need to understand and scruti-
nize model behaviour under noisy supervision in order to establish trust 
and ensure responsible use.
Against this background, granular-ball computing (GBC) introduces 
an innovative multi-granularity processing mechanism that is promising 
for both robustness and interpretability [20]. Its theoretical foundation 
can be traced to information granulation theories such as fuzzy sets and 
rough sets [21], which structure data hierarchically for graded informa-
tion processing. However, these theories are generally applied to simpler 
structures. GBC employs granular-ball (GB) of varying granularity to 
achieve multilevel data segmentation, enabling the model to make clas-
siﬁcation decisions across multiple granularity levels [22]. Unlike tradi-
tional methods, GBC dynamically adjusts the granularity size, adaptively 
extracting information at diﬀerent levels based on data distribution. 
This multilayered processing capability allows the model to disregard 
noise at coarser granularity levels while capturing valuable informa-
tion at ﬁner levels, thereby achieving robust and stable performance on 
noisy datasets [23]. However, existing GBC-based methods, such as the 
Granular-Ball Support Vector Machine (GBSVM) [24], primarily focus 
on enhancing the eﬃciency of traditional classiﬁers by replacing ﬁne-
grained samples with GBs. Unfortunately, these methods often rely on 
rigid clustering techniques, such as the K-means method. This reliance 
limits their ability to handle multimodal or irregularly shaped data dis-
tributions, as the K-means method assumes spherical clusters and equal 
variances, leading to suboptimal granularity adaptation in complex, 
high-dimensional, noisy environments. Furthermore, these methods are 
typically designed for shallow machine learning paradigms and lack 
seamless integration with deep learning architectures, such as CNNs, 
resulting in limited ﬂexibility for noise probabilistic modeling and in-
suﬃcient empirical gains in classiﬁcation accuracy under severe label 
noise.
To address these limitations and ﬁll the identiﬁed research gaps, 
this study introduces Gaussian Mixture-Based granular-ball computing 
(G-GBC) method that integrates GBC with Gaussian Mixture Models 
(GMM) optimized by Mahalanobis distance. This provides a new ap-
proach that leverages the robustness of granular balls and the soft as-
signment mechanism of GMM from a multi-granularity perspective to 
improve the robustness of GBC-based methods in noisy environments. 
G-GBC enhances multi-granularity processing by incorporating proba-
bilistic soft assignments from GMM, which allow for dynamic purity-
weighted adjustments and better preservation of data structures in noisy 
settings. By dynamically adjusting GB granularity and leveraging purity-
weighted assignments, the proposed approach mitigates the impact of 
label noise while preserving critical data structures. The integration of 
this method into CNNs not only improves performance on high-noise 
datasets but also provides enhanced interpretability through visualizing 
the evolution of GB structures during training. These contributions pro-
vide a practical approach to improving robustness and interpretability 
in deep learning models. The main contributions of this paper are as 
follows:
1. We present a novel method to address the challenges associated 
with noisy labels. The proposed method leverages the adaptive clus-
tering capability of GBs to mitigate the adverse eﬀects of misla-
beled data. By dynamically adjusting the GB formation process and 
incorporating noise-tolerant mechanisms, the proposed method ef-
fectively reduces the impact of label noise, enhancing classiﬁcation 
accuracy and robustness in high-noise environments.
2. The proposed adaptive Gaussian mixture-based GBC (G-GBC) 
method uses a Gaussian mixture model (GMM) with Mahalanobis 
distance optimization to accurately capture data distributions. By 
dynamically adjusting the granularity and weight of GBs, the pro-
posed method eﬀectively mitigates the impact of label noise. This 
design enhances the noise resilience of the representation, improv-
ing clustering performance and feature extraction accuracy on high-
noise datasets.
3. The G-GBC method integrates into a CNN framework, enhancing 
both robustness and interpretability. This integration leverages the 
noise-resilient properties of GBs alongside the powerful feature ex-
traction capabilities of CNNs, considerably improving performance 
on noisy datasets. Furthermore, the dynamic visualization of GB 
evolution elucidates the model’s adaptive mechanisms, enhancing 
transparency and interpretability during the training process.
2.  Related work
2.1.  Granular-ball computing
A previous study [25] highlighted that human cognition prioritizes 
the recognition of “broad” contour information in images, introducing 
the concept of “global precedence.” This perspective diﬀers from most 
AI algorithms that rely on ﬁne-grained data points. Building on the abil-
ity of granular computing to partition data and knowledge spaces, Wang 
[26] proposed multi-granular cognitive computing, while Xia et al. [20] 
introduced the idea of using hyperspheres to represent “grains,” lead-
ing to the development of GBC. Further advances, such as the GBSVM 
[24], demonstrated that GBC can enhance eﬃciency and robustness by 
replacing the ﬁnest-grained samples with GBs.
GBC extends this concept by adapting data representation into multi-
granularity GBs, which serve as multi-scale, adaptive units that enclose 
portions of the sample space. Unlike traditional ﬁne-grained methods 
that rely on individual data points or small clusters, GBC leverages 
larger, coarser GBs to capture the essential structure of the data while 
ﬁltering out noise. This allows for more eﬃcient data processing and 
enhanced robustness, as GBC can focus on signiﬁcant patterns at vari-
ous levels granularity, rather than being disrupted by minute variations 
in noisy datasets [27].

points with similar characteristics are enclosed within larger balls, ef-

GBC has shown its versatility in applications such as clustering, 
classiﬁcation, and rough set theory. Al-Hmouz et al. [29] introduced 
granular classiﬁers using multi-granularity levels to enhance classiﬁca-
tion performance, while Slowi´nski [30] combined granular computing

develop robust deep CNN models capable of handling label noise more 
eﬀectively.
2.2.  Learning with noisy labels
The handling of noisy labels has garnered substantial attention in 
recent years, with researchers proposing various eﬀective strategies to 
mitigate the disruptive eﬀects of noise on deep learning models, thereby 
enhancing model robustness and accuracy. Based on the characteris-
tics of these approaches, we classify them into two main categories: 
methods focused on label reﬁnement and robust optimization, which 
directly address noisy labels through correction, robust loss designs, or 
meta-learning techniques; and methods centered on training strategies 
and regularization, which leverage training dynamics and regularization 
techniques to prevent overﬁtting to noise.
2.2.1.  Label reﬁnement and robust optimization methods
These methods focus on improving label quality and optimizing the 
learning process to minimize the impact of noise. Lee et al. [33] pro-
posed CleanNet, a transfer learning framework for scalable image clas-
siﬁer training under label noise, enabling eﬃcient correction through 
prototype-based veriﬁcation. Huang et al. [34] introduced contrastive 
label correction, which enhances noisy label learning by leveraging con-
trastive learning to reﬁne labels based on feature similarities. Tu et al. 
[35] presented a decoupled meta label puriﬁer, separating label puriﬁ-
cation from model training to eﬀectively learn from noisy labels while 
avoiding interference. Liu and Guo [36] introduced peer loss functions, 
enabling eﬀective learning from noisy labels without requiring prior 
knowledge of noise rates by comparing predictions across samples. Wei 
et al. [37] proposed co-regularization within a joint training framework, 
which inherently provides robustness through agreement-based losses.
